speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which I submit affects the rights and privileges of all hon. members of the house. My question of privilege is based upon the report of yesterday's proceedings in the house as recorded in Votes and Proceedings, which I have before me. I have particular reference to the motion for production of papers of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre which was discussed and voted on.
My submission in brief, and I propose to support it by precedents, rulings and other resolutions, is that this report in Votes and Proceedings constitutes a condonation and, more than that, will be a perpetual record of what I submit with respect was a nullity in so far as the proceedings of the house are concerned, or certainly an irregularity, possibly an irregularity which could or might have been cured by the proper record in Votes and Proceedings.
Having made that point, I should like to proceed to establish the question of privilege. The particular motion is one which I think Your Honour and all members will agree is not debatable, and not being debatable it is not susceptible to amendment. There can be no amendment of any such motion for the production of papers. There can be no amendment, of course, because no one can debate the motion; therefore no one can move an amendment.
Over the past number of years, however, a practice has grown up under which ministers of the crown, in dealing with such motions, make certain reservations. These, in fact, constitute amendments. I propose to refer to a ruling to that effect. In spite of that statement, as Your Honour knows, an amendment to the motion can be put with the unanimous consent of the house. It is on that basis that this practice has been enshrined in the proceedings of the House of Commons.
Now I should like to refer Your Honour to a particular motion in 1961 for the production of certain orders made under the
Customs Act. At that time the matter was considered by His Honour Mr. Speaker Michener, and the report of the proceedings is to be found on pages 2439, 2440 and 2441 of Hansard. Mr. Speaker Michener then said very distinctly, and I have the quotation here, that this practice is one which the house accepts, that is of allowing a minister of the crown to accept a motion with reservations, but only on the basis, as he says, of the unanimous consent of the members permitting this to be done. His words in making this ruling are very clear, and I quote:
The other problem, that of amending a motion which is not debatable, has been dealt with by the house by unanimous consent, permitting the ministerial reservation to be expressed by the Chair when the motion is put. In effect a condition is attached to the motion with the unanimous consent of the house before the motion is put.
Now, bearing in mind that ruling, which I think has definitely been accepted through the years, we find in turning to the proceedings of yesterday than when Your Honour put this motion you did so in these words:
Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the said motion subject to the reservations or remarks of the minister?

subtopic: MR. BALDWIN'    REPORT OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE YESTERDAY
speechtext: No.

Not expurgated editions. Produce the record and that is fine.
Subsequently the motion with this reservation was put and was dealt with on that basis. I find on examing Votes and Proceedings, page 73, the motion is set out and then these words appear:
And the question being put, the said motion, subject to the reservations expressed by the Honourable the Secretary of State for External Affairs, was agreed to on the following division:
My submission is that there was not, as is quite apparent from the record, unanimous consent to this motion being put or accepted, with the very vague reservations which the Secretary of State for External Affairs sought to attach. Consequently I suggest that this forms the basis for my proposition that the proceeding was a nullity.
However, this defect might have been cured, because yesterday there was a motion for the production of papers moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam relating to the establishment of a veterinary college. This motion also appears in yesterday's Hansard at page 691. The motion was accepted by the Minister without Portfolio

Question of Privilege
subject to certain reservations. Your Honour put the motion with these reservations, and it was accepted. However, when the motion appeared in Votes and Proceedings no conditions or reservations were attached.
In the limited time available I have searched the Journals of the House of Commons and I have yet to find cases where motions of this kind, with conditions attached such as those sought to be attached by the minister, are recorded in that way. Under those circumstances it is my submission that this particular record as it appears is wrong and should be expunged, of course without prejudice to the right of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to move his motion again if he sees fit to do so.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: MR. BALDWIN'    REPORT OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE YESTERDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the point of privilege raised by the hon. gentleman suggests two points to me. He argues that the proceeding yesterday was a nullity, the proceeding itself was a nullity, and therefore ought to be removed by some method from the records of the house.
I would point out it has been the practice in the house for many, many years to accept these motions subject to reservations which are frequently made by ministers, and that is the form in which the motion was put yesterday, subject to the reservations made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
At that particular time there was an opportunity on the part of any hon. gentleman who felt the privileges of the house were being overlooked, or indeed that order was being overlooked, to register an objection to the proceedings. No such action was taken at that time, and the house proceeded in the normal way to make a decision. A vote was taken and the house accordingly made a decision that these documents should be produced subject to the reservations made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I suggest it is quite improper at this stage to raise a point of privilege on a matter that was dealt with yesterday by the house, with finality, namely by taking a vote. To me that seems to be the substantial point.
With regard to the second point made by the hon. gentleman, that the record of the proceeding in Votes and Proceedings included the phrase "subject to reservations", and that this in some way is not in accordance with past policy, I would point out this is not a substantial point because it has always been understood that a vote taken subject to reservations on a motion for the production of papers, and accepted subject to such reservations, has been reported by the house whether or not the particular qualification was included in Votes and Proceedings. Yesterday was the time to raise the point of

privilege, and it is certainly improper at this time to seek to reverse a decision of the house taken yesterday by a formal vote.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MR. BALDWIN'    REPORT OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE YESTERDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker with respect to the matter of privilege that has been raised, I would say that the Minister of Labour has done us a service by making it clear that there are two points. I agree with the Minister of Labour with respect to the first point. What happened yesterday, happened. We cannot turn back the clock in this house. We learned that once before, some years ago. But with respect to the second point I think the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has a point of privilege when he questions the manner in which the resolution of yesterday is recorded in Votes and Proceedings.
Actually, Mr. Speaker, there were four occasions yesterday when notices of motions for production of papers were passed subject to reservations stated by ministers. This happened in the case of the motion moved by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), in the case of the motion moved by my colleague the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), in the case of the motion moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and it happened in the case of my motion which is now under discussion. If one looks at Votes and Proceedings for yesterday one will discover that in the other three cases there is no reference in Votes and Proceedings to the fact that reservations were made by the ministers concerned. It is only in the case of my motion that this clause is added in Votes and Proceedings.
I might also point out that on Tuesday, May 21, there was before this house a subamendment moved by the leader of this group. On that occasion a vote was called and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) indicated that he was voting for the subamendment on the understanding that it included certain words. There is no reference in Votes and Proceedings of that day to the inclusion of those words; the vote was on the motion as it was put from the chair by Your Honour. I submit, therefore, that the second point raised by the hon. member for Peace River has validity; that it would be a mistake to introduce into Votes and Proceedings, into the official records of this house, this phrase that something has been passed subject to reservations made by ministers.	.
As the Minister of Labour has pointed out, it is a long standing practice-maybe it is one which should have ceased many years ago, but we have had it for a long time-1& accept motions on these conditions, and whefi

we do so the house understands that the return that is later brought down will be brought down in the light of the reservations that have been made.
The Minister of Labour is quite correct; we cannot turn the clock back and re-do what was done yesterday, but the hon. member for Peace River does have the right to raise today the question as to the form in which this incident is recorded in Votes and Proceedings. Hansard, which is not an official record of proceedings, records all the words that were said, but surely what is voted on by the house is the motion that was put, and since no amendment was made there could not be a vote on an amendment.
I think the record in Votes and Proceedings as to what happened to my motion should be the same as the record with respect to the other three motions of yesterday to which I referred, it being the understanding of the house that the reservations recorded in Hansard will be recognized when the document is brought down.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. BALDWIN'    REPORT OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE YESTERDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the point of privilege raised by the hon. member for Peace River I would like to deal with point No. 1, which was not adequately dealt with by the Minister of Labour, who completely omitted any reference to the main point raised by the hon. member, namely that unanimous consent had not been given to the suggested amendment of the motion. It is quite true that the practice of governments and ministers of the crown has been to accept motions with certain reservations which are indicated at the time. The practice over the years has been, as long as I can remember, that the house accepts those reservations without comment, the reservations being restricted to documents which affect other governments or are of such a character that they cannot be disclosed. But in all instances, when a minister of the crown has accepted a motion with the reservations which he has expressed, the Speaker has then asked the opinion of the house and it has been quite normal for the house to agree.
However, in this particular instance-and this is something which has not come to the attention of the house within recent years- when the Speaker asked "Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the said motion subject to the reservations or remarks of the minister?" some hon. members said "No". Obviously at that stage the proceedings deviated from what has been the practice of the house in the past. As a matter of fact, prior to that, when Mr. Speaker said "In the circumstances
Question of Privilege
I shall put the motion subject to the reservation", I myself asked "What reservation?", and the Leader of the Opposition said "What kind of reservation?"
After the second inquiry of Mr. Speaker whether the motion should be adopted subject to the reservation, some hon. members said "No". The Leader of the Opposition intervened and expressed a negative. "Not expurgated editions," he said. "Produce the record and that is fine." At that stage the motion was put to the house.
I suggest to you, sir, that more could hardly have been done. What more could hon. members do than to express a negative in reply to the proposition put before them by Mr. Speaker? At that stage action was required. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the Minister of Labour both said we have missed our opportunity. What should we have done at that particular moment; raised a series of points of order or questions of privilege?
A motion for the production of papers is the same as any other motion, subject to the practice which has prevailed over the years of ministers of the crown adding restrictive reservations. Such a motion would have to be amended in the proper form in the same way all substantive motions are amended before they can be adopted by the house. I think serious consideration will have to be given to this particular record in Hansard or we shall have established a precedent which it will be very difficult to sustain, and which might throw out entirely the practice of the house which has grown up over the years in dealing with these motions for the production of papers.

subtopic: MR. BALDWIN'    REPORT OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE YESTERDAY
speechtext:
There seems to be an essential difference between this motion as passed by the house yesterday and most of those motions which have contained reservations of the kind referred to by other hon. members. Usually such reservations are based on securing the consent of other persons involved with respect to documents whose production is sought. But if I understand the situation which developed yesterday, it is not a matter of obtaining the consent of anyone, except hon. members in the government, before these documents can be produced. It is a matter of discretion on the part of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who made it abundantly clear that the information sought in the motion was probably contained in some documents which he felt he could not reveal in their entirety. Thus when you come to examine this question, Mr. Speaker, I suggest you consider

Question of Privilege
that there is an important distinction attaching to this motion as opposed to motions with respect to which the usual reservations are made.
I wish to make one further point, and in doing so I am in agreement with the Minister of Labour. It was the understanding of the house what the reservations were to be. As a matter of fact several hon. members asked on a number of occasions that these reservations should be spelled out, and, while they may not have been explained to the satisfaction of those hon. members, the house did nevertheless accept the motion on the basis that the reservations had been explained.

subtopic: MR. BALDWIN'    REPORT OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE YESTERDAY
speechtext:
I think this is an important matter for the records of the house because obviously, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Peace River, if we allow it to pass we should perhaps be creating a precedent which would have to receive serious consideration by future Speakers and by the house generally.
I was a little surprised that the Leader of the House did not deal with this question. I recall a matter which was raised last session which I suggest with deference, Mr. Speaker, you may wish to consider. Strangely enough I believe it was the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who moved for the production of papers of a certain kind. I accepted the motion "with the usual reservations" and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, supported by the present leader of the house, immediately fell on me like a ton of bricks and said "What are the usual reservations? We cannot pass this motion with the phrase 'with the usual reservation'. You must define what the usual reservations are." Mr. Speaker Michener took it under consideration and later ruled that the usual reservations "could only be privileged documents or obtaining consent to tabling correspondence".
I think the present house leader made a very strong and undoubtedly a very proper legal argument at that time on that point, and that might be why he is silent today and it might be a precedent, Mr. Speaker, which you would like to consider if you are reviewing this matter further today.

subtopic: MR. BALDWIN'    REPORT OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE YESTERDAY

Mr. Speaker, if Your Honour proposes to take the matter under advisement there is one other feature I should like to point out. I believe that if a reservation is made it should be spelled out in such a way that it can be understood. In this particular case two suggestions were made. The first was that perhaps the minister would produce a summary, and second, perhaps he would produce

extracts. In the end the minister said that he would give consideration to these suggestions, and this is to be found at the bottom of page 689 of Hansard. He said:
I have said that we would give consideration to that. I did not say we would do it.
Mr. Speaker, what I am pointing out is that in my belief, which I expressed following the vote, there was no reservation at all. There was a statement of the minister that he would think something over, and in the result he has put something over. I think that is not uncommon for him. I believe the reservation ought to have been spelled out, and in any case there was no unanimous consent to the motion being put with a reservation.

Mr. Speaker, in connection with this matter I should like to draw to your attention that I think there is very grave doubt as to what we actually voted on yesterday. Personally I was in the position of not knowing on what we were voting, and I think the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) indicated the same thing. As a result, not knowing the implications of the vote, I did not vote yesterday.
However, it seems to me that if we voted on anything, if we paid any attention to the reservations which were expressed, then what we voted on and what was agreed to by the house was that the minister of external affairs would give consideration to two courses of action. I doubt very much that this is a proper type of vote to be taken in the house. Also, as far as the official record is concerned, it shows that the house voted in favour of a motion to produce certain papers which the Secretary of State for External Affairs himself stated could not be produced. Therefore I think we are in an extremely ambiguous situation as far as this vote is concerned, and that the government has put itself in a particularly invidious position.

Mr. Speaker, as I recall it, once before the Speaker ruled on this sort of matter, and it seems to me that the legality of the reservation is taken to be that instead of the hon. member having to go back and amend his motion and put it properly, so the motion for the production of papers will contain the proper reservation, it has been taken that by saying "with the usual reservations" it is an amendment of the motion, and with unanimous consent it can be put in that way.
The point came up before owing to doubt as to the nature of the reservations. Therefore-the previous Speaker usually accepted only those reservations where the house was sure-
JUNE e, 1963
there could not be any misunderstanding as to the type of reservations the motion would contain, and anything other than the usual type of reservations would mean that the motion would have to be withdrawn, and put on the order paper in the proper form to describe exactly on what we were voting, and then the motion could be put. I suggest that the obtaining of unanimous consent is necessary for the handling of a motion for production of papers if it is to be put in anything other than the words in which the motion itself is expressed. I will conclude by referring to the precedent mentioned by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings in reference to a similar occasion when he was asked to define
Question of Privilege
"usual reservations". I think it was perfectly proper for the present house leader and for other hon. members to ask the then minister to specify what "usual reservations" meant, and that was done. speechtext:
It is very simple. It was understood at that time that an attempt was to be made to obtain a legal opinion.

When I was vested with what responsibility I have in this matter, Mr. Dunsmore *came to see me. The house resumed from Wednesday, June 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That a special committee be appointed to consider matters relating to defence and to report from time to time its observations and opinions thereon; that the committee have power to send for persons, papers and records and to examine witnesses; that it be empowered to adjourn from place to place; that standing order 67 be suspended in relation to the committee; and that the committee consist of 24 members to be designated by the house at a later date.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR REPLIES IN FRENCH TO QUESTIONS IN FRENCH
speechtext:
Just prior to the adjournment of the debate last evening I had expressed the concern of the members of this group about the moral aspects of the acceptance of nuclear weapons by the government, and the concern felt by editors and other people in this country. I quoted from an editorial which appeared in the Victoria Times and from another which had appeared in the Vancouver Sun. The article in the Victoria Times referred particularly to the moral burden which was being imposed on the Canadian people by the acceptance of such weapons under these circumstances.
With respect to the military aspects of this question, the futility of this nuclear posture has been well explained by General Simonds, General Macklin, some generals in the United States and other well known authorities. The arguments put forward by these generals and others have been gone into thoroughly by the leader of this group, as well as by others, so there is no necessity to repeat what has been said in that respect. With regard to the economic grounds on which we oppose the acquisition of these weapons, certain increased costs have been incurred which are likely to rise still further when the government gets drawn even deeper into this particular NATO role. I trust the government will look thoroughly into the economic aspects of this acceptance of nuclear weapons.
I think this committee would provide an opportunity to review Canada's role in NATO in the light of changing circumstances. We are little wiser as a result of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization meeting in Ottawa.

Appointment of Defence Committee In fact we have had to rely upon vague communiques which, we were informed fairly reliably, had been drawn up before the meeting was even held in Ottawa, together with certain pious platitudes uttered by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and other members of this government in explanation of what happened at that meeting. To indicate the platitudinous nature of what was put out officially, let me quote briefly what has been said by responsible newsmen who were sent to attend that meeting. On page 57 of United States News and World Report of June 3 four of these correspondents make brief references to their attendance at this conference. The news dispatch reads as follows:
To fill in on the real significance behind all the words at that north Atlantic Alliance meeting just concluded in Ottawa, here is the report of our four member staff on hand for the sessions:
U.S. is going to extraordinary lengths to keep the western alliance from falling apart. At Ottawa, U.S. decided to keep on paying most of the bills for NATO and to avoid showdowns with allies on nuclear strategy or anything else.
Result: there was no firm action on issues long thought pressing.
Hot issues were compromised-or postponed. Differences between allies were soft pedaled. Candor was lacking even in secret talks. Said an insider: "Once again, a crisis has been postponed at the cost of any real progress."
In other words: Need for a forward line of defence in Europe seems much more important to the U.S. than it does to most of its allies on the spot.
Then the communique goes on to say:
In short: U.S., at this time, is unwilling to risk pushing the western alliance into a political crisis. The alliance seems too shaky for that.
So much for the Ottawa meeting. Fact is, Atlantic alliance is in such poor health that several western leaders are administering vitamins.
I think this committee, Mr. Speaker, must be told the facts and the truth about the situation as it is today, and not be content to rest on the information contained in vague communiques and pious platitudes uttered by ministers in the House of Commons, or as my leader has just said, on communiques which were practically completed before the meeting commenced. What a lot of shadow boxing, and at great expense. When NATO was formed the importance of article 2 was stressed and we were treated to syrupy doses of rhetoric on this article, particularly from the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). We placed confidence in the wording of article 2 and accepted the statements that something would be done. However, we all know that nothing aas been done to date to give it effect, although it is a standard ritual at these conferences and annually in this house to pay homage to its value, and so on, and to express hopes with respect to the future.

I am now going to make a few suggestions with respect to questions which should be given careful consideration by the committee. I feel very keenly on this question and so do a good number of Canadians. I have done a lot of reading and have received a pile of correspondence about it. I suggest that the committee should give consideration to the morality of continuing to support some of the leading figures in NATO. During the discussions on German rearmament the present Prime Minister, on January 26, 1955, said this:
The four top men who would have charge of the defence organization they are permitted would be Herr Blank, a trade union leader, Adolf Heusin-ger, never a nazi; Hans Speidel, a German general who was in the plot against Hitler and who was tortured in nazi prisons; while the officer in charge of military education and indoctrination has been described as a man of "glowing conscience" who truly wants to make a new democratic army that belongs to the people.
I think the facts and recent statements by some of these persons indicate that this was a very naive attitude at that time on the part of the present Prime Minister, or he was completely uninformed.
I will give a few illustrations to prove my contention in this respect. Herr Blank was the minister of defence in West Germany at the time of the question of German rearmament. He was also a trade union leader. He was soon replaced by Mr. Strauss, who soon commenced to reveal his true attitude towards NATO. First of all, he surprised and worried all his allies by seeking training ground for German troops in Spain without consultation, second, recently by the arrest of editors of German papers who criticized defence policy. This action was well reported in the German press, and I give credit to the Germans who opposed this action on the part of their minister of defence on the ground that he had little understanding of the workings of democracy.
Then again, I should like to quote from the New York Times of May 15, 1961, an editorial entitled: "Strauss's Nightmare":
No official has been unhappier than Herr Strauss over the recent suggestion in the United States that a Soviet attack should be met with conventional weapons to obtain a 'pause' in the fighting before any nuclear weapons could be employed. "It would give me holy terrors", Herr Strauss said recently during a parliamentary debate on the defence budget, "if I were to hear that a conventional attack was to be met only with conventional weapons, regardless of how big it is, how long it lasts, and what its political aim is."
This is the attitude of a person who acted previously without consulting his allies, and he clearly demonstrates that while his major allies are considering modifying the situation and reducing the risks by talking of using conventional weapons, he is practically saying

that if they were attacked they would use nuclear weapons to repulse that attack.
Then in this morning's Globe and Mail we find that he has agreed to train and equip Nigerian forces, again without consulting his allies. We have to respect the national rights of these people but this is something in the present world situation which should only be undertaken as a result of consultation and action through the United Nations on the basis of collective security. Action like this undertaken by Germany can only result in increasing incidents like those in Katanga. These armed forces can be used to repress the citizens of states who wish to advance the development of democracy, or give effect to the wishes of certain industrialists holding rights over their natural resources, and that sort of thing. I think we have seriously to question where we are going in this respect.
Now I come to a gentleman I mentioned before, on whom I have a large file supplied to me by the American Jewish congress, who supplied the same documents to Senator Morse in 1961. This is General Adolf Heusinger. The Prime Minister said that he was never a nazi. By George, if you read the record you will find he did all of the things the worst of the nazis were accused of doing.

Mr. Speaker, the house is discussing a matter of tremendous importance to our country and to the freedom of the free world. The numbers in the house would not give that indication, but the fact is that this is one of those debates in which each and every one of us who will not be on the committee in any event should have an opportunity of placing our views before the house and the country. If I had any doubt as to the need for my participation in this debate, it was removed this afternoon by the most unusual series of answers given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) regarding this very important question of nuclear weapons.
This committee, he said, would consider the whole question of the nuclear force. As I recall, and of course I have not seen the actual words, he said that no decision regarding that force in Europe would be made until a full discussion had taken place in this committee. Then, when I asked him a question I received from him an answer that becomes more surprising the longer the time passes between the answer that was given and the consideration I have been able to give to it. He said, in effect that, different from the previous government, this government emphasizes the greater role of conventional than nuclear weapons in NATO.
Now this, to me, is a most surprising statement, a statement that cannot be made to fit the suggestions made by the Prime Minister both during and since the election campaign. He said, in effect, that it was a hypothetical question, but perhaps the position differs because his government emphasizes the importance of conventional defences for NATO. This certainly wiped away all the

Appointment of Defence Committee policies regarding nuclear weapons. The statement has no basis in fact. I should like to know how that statement can be made to coincide with the undertaking, apparently entered into by this government, to supply our air force in Europe with bombs of an explosive power of one billion tons of t.n.t. These aircraft, 144 in number, are to be equipped, according to one who certainly in the past was not far removed from the ear of the Liberal party-I refer to the president of the exchequer court-with bombs of an explosive power which indicate that no longer are these weapons defensive, but they are aggressive in effect.
I should like to hear some of these proponents, these pundits, give their explanation for the somersault turned by the Prime Minister today in this regard. I could not understand it. What has happened? What has come over the Prime Minister for him to make a statement, in effect, that if a decision is taken, and I underline "if", it need not involve any additional expenditures. My question referred to the new system for which Mr. Merchant is here as the vendor. He said that the new system need not involve any additional expenditures at all because, in effect, it might result in a diversion of expenditures from one form of defence to another.
This is a strange doctrine, a strange and unusual answer. On the one hand, according to Mr. Justice Thorson, they are going to equip the aircraft in Europe with bombs of an explosive power of one billion tons of t.n.t., and on the other hand the Prime Minister says that we may be changing over; that we believe in a greater extension of conventional arms. I want to hear his explanation in this connection when he replies at the end of this debate.
Now, the questions and answers today indicate to me more clearly than ever the need for the fullest discussion in respect of this committee, so that the membership of this house will be able to place before parliament and the country their views on this most important, most significant question. Do not let anyone say we should not debate the subject because we must get on. The zero hour for the 60 days approaches. There is no question of obstruction, but there is the necessity for the fullest discussion, and that necessity is increased by the answer given which is, within the realm of parliamentary language, a sinuous disregard of the facts.
Ever since parliament opened, I have been waiting to hear about the commitment made by the government which I had the honour to head. They have snooped; they searched;

they have sought and they have found nothing. In that connection, let me say that I am sure the Prime Minister is greatly impressed by anything the Toronto Star may say. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Leader of the Opposition, if he would permit a question. The question is: how does he regard the Columbia river treaty as being delivered when it has a condition in it that it must be ratified by parliament in Ottawa?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR REPLIES IN FRENCH TO QUESTIONS IN FRENCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so far as the
United States and Canada are concerned it is signed, sealed and delivered, and all treaties require to be accepted by parliament or confirmed by parliament in the constitutional manner. Now they are trying to get around certain of the provisions in such a way as will render unnecessary the submission of that treaty to the United States congress again.
Then the report goes on to say this:
Though it was never ratified-
The hon. gentleman has his answer in the next paragraph. Apparently he has not read this issue of the Star.
Though it was never ratified by parliament, the treaty was signed by the Diefenbaker government. Yet Mr. Pearson has had no hesitation in pressing the United States to renegotiate for terms more acceptable to Canada. Was this dishonourable?
Then it goes on to say:
-let it be clearly recognized that Canada has not now-and has never had-any treaty obligation under NATO to accept nuclear arms. In fact, under the NATO treaty signed in April, 1949, we are not even committed to supply any specific number of troops or equipment for the alliance.
Then it goes on to say this regarding commitments:
Was the United States dishonourable when, for practical military and economic reasons it cancelled its "commitment" to supply Britain with the Skybolt air-to-ground missile?
Finally it concludes:
In short, Canada has no commitment to accept nuclear arms. And even if we had, there should be no hesitation in spurning it if we consider it in the national interest to do so.
If the Pearson government is convinced we should get nuclear arms, let it justify the weapons on their merits if any. But let it stop trying to tell the Canadian people it's all the fault of the Diefenbaker administration.
Mr. Speaker, I could not place before the house the unprejudiced opinion of any newspaper more powerful and more effective than that which I have now placed before the house.

Oh yes, indecision, but not one suggestion as to what the policy of the Liberal government is. We have had to get the clarification from the Prime Minister today, that now they are going in the direction of non-nuclear armaments. I shall come back to this, because I have a number of questions to propound.
The committee was promised by the Prime Minister in these 60 days of decision. He said they were going to take the whole problem of defence and bring it before the committee. On March 26, speaking at Kingston, he said that a Liberal government would set up an all party House of Commons defence committee to take the defence issue away from partisan politics. The committee's work would

Appointment of Defence Committee be part of a Liberal government's review of Canadian defence policy to determine an appropriate role for this country, but such changes would also take considerable time. There is no doubt about that; no decision is going to be made for a considerable time. Now, before the committee is set up, and the government having made that solemn undertaking, it has committed Canada to a strategic force in NATO equipped with bombs of an explosive power to which I have already referred.
The major matter for decision is determined by the government without any consideration by parliament, without any discussion before parliament and, above all, in a manner that denies the carrying into effect of the promise made by the Prime Minister that this committee would make a determination on the question of policy. This is nothing unusual; I have noted it in the question period. I have noted in other particulars a number of examples since the new government took office of its inheritance of that spirit of insolence and arrogance which characterized the former Liberal government of Canada.
What are they going to place before the committee? An accomplished fact, in so far as the agreement made in NATO is concerned. What recommendations are they going to receive from the committee? They are simply going to advise the committee that they entered into certain arrangements and undertakings at the NATO meeting and they will be carried out. Sir, I want to make very clear that we in Her Majesty's loyal opposition do not intend to be hamstrung from asking questions in parliament, demanding information and discussing defence while this committee is sitting. We are not going to have this committee used as a makeshift. The Prime Minister said in his speech at Kingston that it will take a long time to do this, and during that period of time we intend that in no way shall we be denied the opportunity of placing our views fully before the house and asking such questions as we deem proper, regardless of whether or not the committee is sitting.
I mentioned the Minister of National Defence a moment ago. He says he has a great deal of information on a number of things. Speaking in the house in January or early February he stated that he was not going to be tied down by classified information. Why, he had been to Europe. He was over there; he saw General Norstad. They sat down together; they talked, and he learned. When he came back he said, "I am not going to be stifled. I am going to tell you what I know". Well, he did not tell us much then,

and he certainly did not tell us very much the other day, regarding the defence policies of the Liberal party, this carefully developed program to which the Prime Minister referred in his Kingston speech. He said:
The Liberal party is not approaching the problems of government blindly. We have a carefully developed program of definite, concrete policies.
Then a little later in that speech he said:
I further pledge that as soon as parliament meets we will act to bring the muddle and confusion on defence to an end. We will fulfil Canada's defence commitments to our allies. Then, so that the critical issue of defence may be removed from partisan politics, I repeat as a pledge that we will establish an all-party defence committee of the House of Commons.
The NATO conference met. What was decided, other than that Canada undertook commitments which she had never had before?

Mr. Pearson's Toronto statement was a complete reversal of his previously expressed opinion and of former declared Liberal policy.
Then he went on to say this:
For example, on January 13, 1961 he said to a Liberal rally at Ottawa:
"We must speak and act firmly when our rights are threatened by American action".
Who was anti-American then? Mr. Justice Thorson went on to say in his speech that the Prime Minister said:
"We must not be the echo or satellite of any other state".
Who was anti-American then? He went on to quote the Prime Minister as saying:
"Specifically we should not acquire or use nuclear weapons under any kind of national or j oiut control".
Then Mr. Justice Thorson said:
Even as late as November 14, 1962 he-
That is, the Prime Minister:
-stated that he had "always maintained that Canadians should not accept nuclear weapons under either national control or jointly with the United States".
Mr. Justice Thorson continued:
This was declared Liberal policy until Mr. Pearson changed it on January 12, 1963. Small wonder, therefore, that the Canadian campaign for nuclear disarmament was disappointed with his new stand and shocked by it-

Then he goes on to deal in general with the whole problem and he says:
According to a recent press report, it has been proposed that in the course of performing their strike reconnaissance function the Starfighters should carry a one megaton hydrogen bomb. When I read of this proposal I felt impelled by a sense of duty not to "keep silence" but to speak in protest against it. That is why I appear before you this evening. The proposal is a monstrous one. It ought to be repudiated immediately.
Then he goes on and uses this language. He is not a Conservative or a former Conservative, but is one of those who sat with hon. gentlemen opposite:
And the proposal, if the press report is correct, that Canada's Starfighters should become "first-strike" bombers carrying a one megaton hydrogen bomb is an iniquitous one.
The implications of such a proposal are staggering.
Then he summed up this question. He had long years of experience in the House of Commons and in government. He went on to say this, and this is my answer to the government when they say they were carrying out commitments of ours:
A one megaton bomb is not a weapon of defence. It could be an instrument of mass murder.
Then he said:
There is room for argument that a distinction may be drawn between equipping our Bomarc missiles and our Voodoo interceptors in Canada and our Honest John rockets in NATO with nuclear weapons on the one hand, and providing hydrogen bombs for our Starfighters for their strike reconnaissance role on the other, on the ground that the former are defensive tactical weapons and the latter are clearly not.
What brought this about? We were not to be a satellite and we were to stand up for ourselves. Then, even before the NATO meeting, the Canadian government had capitulated to the extent that these tactical forces in Europe were being equipped with offensive weapons. Why did not the government wait until the committee was set up? This is the most important decision that has been made in these 60 days of decision; and yet no opportunity is given, as was undertaken, for a discussion in and a recommendation from this committee.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) mentioned a moment ago some of the matters that could have been dealt with at the NATO meeting, and were not. I listened to the Prime Minister speaking from the podium here. How many of the ideas that he placed before NATO were accepted? I know of none. Was there any advance made to have article 2 of the NATO treaty implemented? Was there any stand taken on the part of the Canadian government in the field of defence with regard to the standardization and co-operative construction of weapons-production sharing as part of 28902-5-48
6, 1963
Appointment of Defence Committee defence? Was anything done in that connection? Apparently all that was done at that NATO meeting was the making by Canada of a voluntary offer to provide tremendous bomb explosive power for her Starfighters in Europe. I know of no other stand which was taken, except the allocation of a nebulous force to which some reference can be made in a moment. What about this important question of sharing and production? No one ever did more in this regard than the Hon. Raymond O'Hurley as minister of defence production. He said to the United States- and he made it very clear-that we would join together in defence, which meant that each of us must make a contribution and must have an opportunity, industrially, to do so. What was the result? Well, in 1961, United States orders in Canada totalled $142 millions. Canadian orders in the United States amounted to $94 millions. We reversed the old order. In 1962 we received orders from the United States amounting to $254.3 millions and the United States received orders from Canada totalling $127.4 millions.
There has been a new policy declared by the United States since the present government came to office. Under this new policy, Mr. McNamara has issued a directive calling for the elimination of all purchasing abroad. Canada is not excluded from the terms of that directive. What is being done by the present government in this connection? At the present moment, the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Drury) is in Washington. Is he going to insist, as we insisted, and with success, that Canadian industry should receive its fair proportion of the joint production program of our two countries, or is the recent declaration by Washington one that will kill the sharing program and deal a severe blow to Canadian industry? We have no information in this regard. Strangely enough, at the NATO meeting this was one of the subjects which normally would have been discussed but which, apparently, was not discussed. I do not intend to go into the subject of the NATO meeting, except to say, as the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) said a few moments ago, that the communique-and this has been reported over and over again-was born and produced before the meeting even began. There is proof of this available. A strange meeting. They bring the representatives of 15 countries together, and they know in advance what they are going to decide. No wonder you can get unity in those circumstances. What about the defence studies? Did the communique mean much? I do not know who these Canadian officials are who give

Appointment of Defence Committee press reports, but Mr. Dave McIntosh is certainly one who writes with authority and information, and he says:
The Canadian government gives every indication that it would rather never have heard of the proposed NATO seaborne strategic nuclear force.
The reason is obvious: Prime Minister Pearson has often said Canada could not get mixed up in the strategic weapons business.
I should like to know what kind of a weapon that million ton explosive bomb could be described as being.
The article says that the conference communique which came out of that meeting was disappointing to Canadian officials and goes on to give the reasons why there was really nothing accomplished. The countries which attended did, however, bring about a force, un-named and, as yet, unsung-a force to bring together various contingents, the United States to supply the Polaris weapons, the British to supply their bombers and so on. The French accept this because they feel it does not mean very much. They had no objection to a nuclear force being established and will provide two air wings as long as the force is not supranational. I should like to know why Canada has rushed in with these undertakings before the setting up of this committee to consider so important a matter. I should like the Prime Minister to explain what advance has been made in negotiations with the United States for an agreement regarding nuclear weapons for the NATO force. Is it not a fact that four of those eight squadrons are stationed in France and four in Germany, and that France will not allow the storage of nuclear weapons in France. This was brought to the attention of the country by Mr. Clement Brown in an article which appeared toward the end of May. What is being done in this regard? Are .we to have four squadrons in France with the necessary nuclear deterrent stored in Germany or in Belgium? How does the government intend to go about this? Is the right hon. gentleman entering into an agreement? The minister of defence (Mr. Hellyer) has not heard about this, apparently. He laughs. Every time I hear or see him in the house I am reminded of "The Deserted Village", the lines-
And still they gaz'd, and still the wonder grew,
That one small head could carry all he knew.
Every time the hon. gentleman speaks I think of Goldsmith. I ask him this: why did he not give us this information? Since France has not accepted nuclear warheads even under the double key system, is Canada to be prevented by France from storing American nuclear weapons on French soil? Has there been any discussion in this regard? The matter is complex and difficult. It is one

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-5, to amend the Bankruptcy Act (primary products under processing).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am bringing Bill No. C-5 into this house only on account of the hardships which are created or enforced on people in Canada who are producers of primary products owing to the present legislation, which I think is too unfair, one-sided and undemocratic. This bill is self-explanatory, as I am sure you will agree with me when you read the bill and explanatory notes. I feel, as do many people, that it is high time we quit treating banks as tender little babies, and this is what I mean by one-sided legislation. We all know that little babies have to be coddled and pampered to make sure they survive, and that this is necessary because they are helpless. 1 might say here that I know this is so because we have one of our own four weeks old.
To say that our banks are helpless is far from the truth. They are protected by section 88 of the Bank Act, and I should like to read the explanatory notes at this point, if I have your permission, Mr. Speaker.
JUNE e, 1963
This bill proposes to prevent the financial distress suffered by unpaid primary producers when the processor in possession of their products goes bankrupt. In many cases the processor has obtained a loan by pawning these products to a bank under a blanket or floating lien: in effect, the processor gambles with the credit of the producer as risk capital-the bank clothed in the blanket protection of the producer's assets secured by section 88 of the Bank Act, the processor diapered with the limited liability of the Bankruptcy Act, while the primary producer goes bare of assets and stripped of credit.
This bill would remedy the grievance by removing primary product assets from the assets in bankruptcy and by providing that such assets, whether improved or unimproved, be sold by the court designated under the Bankruptcy Act. The rights of labour are protected by reserving to the employees a three month lien for wages; thereafter the balance is distributed fairly among the producers and, as to any balance, to the trustee in bankruptcy for distribution to the creditors subject to any lien held by a bank or by the industrial development bank. In this way the producer is protected as to his product and credit, the employee for his hire, the processor (and his creditors) for his managerial contribution, and the bank for its credit advances.
I would ask all hon. members to consider these plain facts as are outlined here. We have had too many of these inefficient operators go bankrupt, and by doing so they have jeopardized the livelihood of a good many families of primary producers in our country, whether they be primary producers of products from the land, forest, sea, quarry or mine. When these producers lose their assets they may have been trying to educate their children, make payments on a mortgage, and meet other commitments necessary to their way of life; but under the present legislation all this is lost. Most of the time the banks come out ahead of the game; we well recognize the fact that they are much better off than the primary producer.
I should like to refer to one such case of bankruptcy in our area, with which I am familiar. This occurred last year and concerned a processor of fruits and vegetables who went bankrupt. Before our marketing organization authorized this person to hold a licence they wrote to his bank to find out whether he was worthy and financially responsible to operate a company of this type. The bank wrote back and intimated that he was O.K financially, fully knowing that his borrowings at that time were 100 per cent of his assets. It almost appears as though the bank hoped to allow him to get back into business long enough to contract for the crops, process them, and then hope to walk in, as they did in fact, and put him into receivership when the crops were processed and in the can. Mr. Speaker, if you were a primary producer of products would you not think that this was a sort of planned conspiracy?
These producers of primary products grow their crops, which in turn they harvest and 28902-5-48i
Bankruptcy Act
then deliver, fully hoping they will be paid for the crops they have produced. Many of them have thousands of dollars invested in such things as fuel, fertilizer, plants, spraying equipment, and wages for harvesting which can amount to well over 50 per cent, in many cases, of the gross return on a crop. I know of one of these young farmers in my area who last year went into debt on account of this. He had a 100-acre fruit farm and it was free and clear of all encumbrances. Last year he suffered frost damage in his orchards and again this year. He harvested only half his crop, but he incurred practically the same expenses as he would had he harvested his complete crop. By this I mean that he had all his spraying and cultivation expenses, and everything else which goes along with harvesting a fruit crop, except the cost of picking the crop. His total cost, which he borrowed from the bank for his operation, was $19,000. What he was supposedly to have received or should have received from the processor amounted to approximately $20,000. He got nothing at all for his crop, but he had to pay the bank. The bank makes sure that they get paid, do not forget that. He now has a $20,000 mortgage on his farm. I should say at this point that he could not obtain this money from the federal government because they did not see fit to lend this type of money in that area. He is paying a higher rate of interest than on an ordinary loan from the Canadian Farm Credit Corporation. He should never have had to incur this debt on account of someone else's inefficiency. This is plainly obvious to anybody. I checked this with all kinds of small processors. I never bothered the big ones because they do not operate under this section. The small processors told me that they are 100 per cent in favour of this act being amended.
I should also like to point out why these inefficient processors who go broke create problems for the efficient processor, whether he be small or large. When these inefficient processors go broke the food brokers are generally waiting to get this produce as cheaply as possible so as to depress the price of the other canned processed goods which are similarly sold by the efficient processors, and thus disrupt, if they can, the whole market. The worst thing about it is that the consumers very rarely get any benefit from this. It is a real racket.
I ask all hon. members: Do they think they should be able to borrow money on my house, my car, my farm or any of my assets without my having anything to say about it? This is actually what is happening. The primary producer of these products, whether they be from the land, sea, mine or forest, has little if anything to say about it. I would

Bankruptcy Act
have no objection if the primary producer had anything to say about the processor borrowing money on the producer's assets, but at the present time he has nothing whatsoever to say about it.
I would ask hon. members to keep this point in mind. How many of us can borrow 10 per cent of our assets as this processor I mentioned earlier borrowed from a bank? A farmer has a fat chance of borrowing any more than about 10 per cent of his assets.
One of the reasons that the primary producer cannot claim these assets after the processor gets them is that he loses identification with his product. Tomatoes go into a can and it is pretty hard to say whose tomatoes they are. Peaches, pears and other vegetables go into cans and it is pretty hard to say "that is my product". A stonecutter cuts raw stone which may go into building stones or tombstones and it is pretty hard to say which is his stone if the processor goes bankrupt. The same is true of coal or pulp-wood. In the case of pulpwood it is hard for the producer to identify his pulpwood when it is transformed into newsprint. The primary producer is faced with a most difficult stumbling block in trying to prove identification of his product. I ask all hon. members for their co-operation in giving this bill second reading.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased on behalf of the Social Credit party, to say that we support the principle of Bill C-5, an act to amend the Bankruptcy Act.
Being myself a manufacturer, I understand very well what this bill is aiming at. We cannot but support the measure and see to it that it is adopted. Moreover, we are happy to note that it is presented by a member of the party in power.
Mr. Speaker, this bill proposes to protect the suppliers of primary goods by forcing a company to take the necessary measures to protect the advances made.
At the present time, section 88 of the Bank Act allows them to accept as a first mortgage the goods supplied on credit by the manufacturers who, on the other hand, are not subject to any restriction with regard to the goods they themselves supply on credit to other manufacturers.
We also know that the chartered banks are fully protected in regard to their loans to those firms, taking as collateral goods which are still unpaid and which were supplied by the producer of primary goods.

I believe it would be fitting to pass Bill C-5 as it stands now in order to protect the claims of small suppliers, just as the banks are protected under section 88 of the Bank Act. In fact, I believe that is what the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Whelan) had in mind when he moved this bill, that is the protection of the suppliers who, at present, stand to lose money in case of bankruptcy by the manufacturers who are not subject to any credit restriction.

I thank the hon. member opposite for his interjection on my behalf. The pearls of wisdom that I offer here should be heard clearly by all.
I would point out that here is a case where the producer of the primary products referred to in the bill is not well protected in our economy as it is constituted. There is a basic premise when one is buying a house or a car: Let the buyer beware. If you go to buy a car you should take a good look at the engine and make sure it will run. If you get it home and it does not run too well, most times it does not do too much good to run to your lawyer with your troubles because he is going to tell you that you should check before you buy. Let the buyer beware.
In our economy as a whole I think this is a fairly sound precept and it is to some degree fundamental in a free enterprise economy that people do in large measure look after their own interests, protect themselves and do what is best individually for their own private businesses and private interests. However, in this twentieth century, in this age of big government, big interests, big business, I think we often come to the pass where the game is not an even or fair game.
The big interests in looking after their own well-being, economic and otherwise, as is their right in a free enterprise system, have the very best of information, advice and professional help available to them. The result is that gradually over the course of the years they have, through this kind of help and through this kind of good business practice, got the game weighted too much in their own favour so that it is no longer a fair or even game and so that the person who is not organized on a broad, powerful and corporate economic basis cannot compete fairly and evenly in the game. No matter how he bewares before he buys, he is going to get caught because the rules of the power game are stacked against him. I think the type of situation that we have here is one which is prevalent in bankruptcy proceedings.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the bankruptcy laws as they are now constituted are little more than a vehicle created by the federal government to enable fraud. How many examples have we seen of absolute fraud sheltering under the benign aegis of the federal bankruptcy laws? I understand that during the last parliament, before my advent here, there was a proposal by the then minister of justice-I think it would be in order for me to say here, even though I sit on this side of the house, he was a most outstanding
Bankruptcy Act
minister of justice-to amend the bankruptcy laws to counteract some of the inequities contained in them. Unfortunately, his bill was never brought before the house. Certainly it was never made law. It appears that there were matters that occurred in this house which interfered somewhat with such humble legislation as bankruptcy laws, and the then minister of justice departed for greener fields before he could bring this bill to fruition.
It is my hope that the bill proposed by the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Whelan) will alleviate some of the hardships imposed on the primary producers whom he has defined so adequately in the definition section of the bill. It is my hope that the bill will provide some protection to those people who supply primary materials or labour for a project, when bankruptcy ultimately occurs. We are not doing anything very radical. I do not believe we are doing anything very socialistic-if the word "socialistic" is a bad word and I do not know that it is. All we are doing is creating a preference similar to the type of preference that has already been given to banks under section 88. I think it might be compared to the type of preference that is given to the supplier of materials or labour under the provincial mechanics lien legislation.
I think we know that under the provincial mechanics lien legislation, if the supplier of labour or materials carries out the provisions of that legislation, he has a priority over other persons to the extent of the labour or materials supplied. Surely, all we are doing here is carrying that sound, fundamental precept that the person who supplies the original goods or labour should be the fellow at the top of the heap instead of putting the fellow who supplies the financing always at the top of the heap. If the provincial legislature has seen fit to give that type of priority to this fundamental supplier of materials or labour, then surely in so far as the bankruptcy aspect is concerned, which is the federal aspect of this same type of problem, we should see fit to give that same type of priority or preference to the supplier of labour or primary products as opposed to the supplier of finance, who is now the fellow who holds the sacrosanct spot at the top of the financial totem pole.
I think that this bill attempts to do so, and it does so very well. It is a well conceived and well thought out measure. I feel it solves that fundamental problem. I do not see that any basic wrong will be done. It is always a problem when we are trying to right one wrong in some segment of the

Bankruptcy Act
economy to make sure that we do not create another wrong in some other segment of the economy.
Let us assume that we are dealing with the perfect economic man that the economics professors so dearly love. Let us assume he is entering into some contract-and I shall use the same illustration as my hon. friend used-to provide tombstones. He is a small supplier of tombstones. At the present time, how does he protect himself to make sure he does not supply these tombstones to a person or a corporation whose financial status is shaky, and to make sure that in the event of bankruptcy he will have some protection? Furthermore, how does he make sure he is not doing business with a financially shaky person or institution? Well, to the best of my knowledge, it is very difficult, if not impossible, for the supplier of tombstones to ascertain if anyone has a section 88 lien with the particular person with whom he is doing business.
It may be that if he hires a costly and expert lawyer

I find all lawyers are costly whether or not they are expert-he may be able to find out whether or not there is a section 88 loan. However, fundamentally, a section 88 loan is a private financial arrangement between the banker and his client. It is not the subject matter of public notice. He might be able to find out if somebody has a chattel mortgage, and the holder of that mortgage would have a prior right to the tombstone supplier in the event of bankruptcy. He would have to search the appropriate registry office to ascertain this. If he goes to all this expense of hiring the necessary accountants and lawyers, then he had better go down to the provincial capital and find out if there is any prior registration under the corporation securities registration which would put the corporation securities on the financial totem pole ahead of the supplier of tombstones. I suggest right here that if he is going to do all this, spend all this money each time he sells a tombstone, then he is going to have to get a very big price for this tombstone in order to pay the lawyers and accountants. Then, by the time he gets all this research done the poor fellow who is looking for the tombstone may be dead, and buried too.
I suggest, therefore, that today, no matter how vigilant, or how good a businessman the primary supplier may be, there is no way in which he can carry on his business in a practical fashion and find out whether or not the person with whom he is doing business is a good risk. If my hon. friend's bill is made law, I suggest this process is going to be made easier. These institutions, these banks and

finance companies will have to protect themselves. These huge financial entities have resources which enable them to protect themselves in a way that the small, individual producer is not able to do today. I have no vendetta against the banks or finance companies. There are times, such as when it comes time to pay election bills, when I am very glad to have them as friends to make me a loan to carry me over the next four years.
I do not want to get the bankers mad at me, because they are apt to bring down that axe that is hanging so precariously over the back of my neck right now.
I believe that in this particular case there will be no great wrong done to these financial institutions that are an essential part of our economic structure. I think that they will be able to protect themselves in making loans and in doing business. Maybe it will make them a little sharper, a little more careful. Maybe they will look into matters more carefully than they do now, because now they can get a section 88 lien and whether things go badly or not, they are all right. This may make them even more efficient in doing their business, now that the banks and financial institutions realize we are always behind Mr. Primary Producer, and that we are always behind the supplier of labour and materials. Therefore in financing these projects they had better be certain (a) that the man running the show is sound financially, that he is able to carry out his business and, (b) see to it that he stays in business, or otherwise they may be at the bottom of the heap, and the primary producers who supply the goods are the only ones who may get their money.
In doing so I think the banks may be able to play a bigger part in helping these individual financial ventures to prosper and go ahead. There was a day when our bankers used to be a sort of partner to small business. The banker used to help the small businessman in planning his future, planning his growth, and the day to day administration of his business; but today with these great areas of protection for the banks, such as section 88, the banker no longer has to be a partner, because he is like a sheriff with his hands on the businessman's throat. If things go badly, he is not in the old time position of being a partner and friend of the small businessman.
Through this bill my hon. friend is trying to play a great part in enabling the banker to get back on an even basis with the primary producer. In so doing we may not only be doing a favour in this question of bankruptcy as it affects the small business community but we may be helping in some way to reestablish that partnership-I think we could
JUNE e, 1963
call it that walking together on an even footing-of the small businessman and the banker, which is essential to our small business community, rather than have all the power and all the rules geared in favour of the banks.
Therefore it gives me great pleasure to support this bill introduced by my hon. friend from Essex South and I commend him for presenting it to the house. It is a very salutary type of legislation which will help our small businessmen to prosper.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Whelan) for introducing a bill that will give some protection to the primary producers against the provisions that are contained in section 88 of the Bank Act. However, I think there is another illustration that should be brought to the attention of the house, and which has not been pointed out thus far in the debate.
I was rather intrigued by the illustration that was so well explained by the hon. member for Essex South and then expanded on by the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene), regarding the manufacture of tombstones. There is another possible involvement, if I may put it that way, that the primary producer occasionally gets into, and that is in the matter of supplying primary products for the manufacture and the processing of goods whereby he enters into an agreement under which he does not expect to receive payment until the finished product is sold. This of course lengthens out the time before he receives payment.
This makes the provisions of this bill even more important to the primary producer because, on a straight business deal where he supplies primary products and expects to be paid on, for example, a 30 day basis whether the finished products are sold or not, then if the primary producer is not paid, within a very short space of time he can at least attempt to take some action. This is in contrast with those occasions where primary producers have supplied primary products going into the manufacture of goods. Several months have gone by, during which they did not expect any further interim payment; and by the time their suspicions were aroused and they got around to doing something about collecting, they found themselves in the position where legal action had been taken and the provisions of section 88 of the Bank Act made it impossible for them to gain.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Renfrew South because if I understood him correctly he placed no reservations on his acceptance of the provisions
Bankruptcy Act
of the bill. Therefore if he were the spokesman for his party I would assume they are prepared to accept the bill, allow it to come to a vote and be passed. I certainly hope that is the intention of hon. members of the Liberal party, because on a good many occasions we have heard government supporters speak in glowing terms of some of the provisions of a private member's bill or resolution, but add that they had one or two reservations and on account of those reservations they said it would be best to take another look at the particular measure proposed.
If this bill in its entirety meets the viewpoint of the Liberal party then I suggest, instead of following the usual procedure of talking such bills out, they let it come to a vote so that its beneficial provisions can become effective.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR REPLIES IN FRENCH TO QUESTIONS IN FRENCH
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PAYMENT TO PRODUCERS OF PRIMARY PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to support this bill introduced by the hon. member for Essex South I do so in almost fear and trembling following shortly after the hon. member for Renfrew South. However as I am a primary producer myself I would like to deal with the bill from that viewpoint.
As we all know, the bill is not pointed towards the efficient canner or producer, and there is no one in the house who wants to take advantage of a small industry just starting, whether it be a canning industry or something else. If I remember correctly it has been said that if all the small industries across Canada each employed one person there would be practically no unemployment in the country. So, we are not against that principle; but we are against them if they are going to start their industries at the expense of the primary producers.
We all know what canners' contracts are. You contract to sell your crop to the canners or the processors and you receive your money in the fall. There is absolutely no money put down and there is no guarantee that moneys will be paid before the fall. So it means that a grower or a primary producer of no matter what, whether it be pulp, vegetables or fruit, has to carry the total cost of growing his crop and harvesting it.
I do not know how many hon. members are practical growers, whether in fruit or vegetables, but I do know that when the average grower starts out-I will take tomatoes just as an illustration-he has his plants to buy. Then they have to be planted. There is then the fertilizing situation, and anybody who knows anything about fertilizing knows

Bankruptcy Act
that ii they are to grow a crop they have to put a lot of money into fertilizing, depending upon the size of the crop. Then there are spraying costs. I do not know whether hon. members realize it, but in the spraying of apples alone I have put on as high as 18 complete sprays in one season, and the average is 14. When I say complete, I mean complete; that is, on each side of the tree. With regard to tomatoes, a few years ago there was no such thing as spraying but today you spray four to eight times. I am trying to point out these costs to the house. Then there are the harvesting costs. With regard to all these costs there is no guarantee whatsoever that the individual will receive one penny if the processor goes broke.
The hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Whelan) cited a case or two. I would like to cite the case of a very elderly couple. They have not yet reached the age at which they draw the old age pension. This couple had a large family and it took every cent of their earnings to educate these young people and get them going. They had ten acres on which they tried to do all these things and make a living. They did a very fine job, because they were a very frugal couple. They had five acres of tomatoes in, and those five acres meant their livelihood that year. The canning factory went broke and they were left without a cent. Is that democracy? Are we living in a democratic country if we allow such things to happen?
All I want to say to the house is, let us support this bill. It may be that the odd flaw will have to be straightened out, but let us give the primary producer and the small grower an even chance.
