speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my support to the bill and to congratulate the hon. member from Essex South (Mr. Whelan) for having brought this measure to our attention. When the discussion commenced I was not familiar with the background of the bill or the requirements for it, but the speeches that have been made this evening have certainly convinced me and, I am sure, all members of our group that this is a proposal worthy of support.
We feel there are some qualifications about the bill. The definition seems unusually wide, and we have some qualms about the actual wording of the legislation; but no doubt these can all be resolved at the committee stage. I understand that there is an informal agreement that this measure is to come to a vote. Speaking for our party and, I hope, for many other hon. members, we are delighted to see this approach being taken.
I think this bill is a very excellent illustration of the proposals that were placed before the house when the first private

members' measures were brought before us for consideration. This is a proposal that is very meritorious and deserving of support. However, it does need to be examined a little more closely at the committee stage. Witnesses should be heard from, and perhaps a slightly more expanded bill brought back for consideration at a later time. Mr. Speaker, we are delighted to see private members' bills actually coming to a vote. This is something that I know all new members have wanted to see very much, because all the private members' measures on the order paper have good ideas in them and most of them will, I am sure, receive the support of the house and go to committee where they can be properly examined.
To me this is a very refreshing departure from the farcical treatment that private members' bills have received in this house in the past. On my own behalf and, I am sure, on behalf of all the members of our party, I want to congratulate you, sir, on taking this constructive stand. It is obvious that the fact this measure is coming to a vote is a bit of a surprise to everybody, because the house is almost empty. However, if this procedure continues to be followed and some of our more unusual and radical bills come up for a vote, I am quite sure that private members' hour could become one of the most exciting, stimulating and best attended periods of the House of Commons and could become a time when new, radical, different and fresh ideas could be considered and actually voted upon. As I have said, private members' hour could become one of the best periods of our discussions here.
So, Mr. Speaker, basically we endorse the bill. We congratulate the hon. member from Essex South for having brought this matter to our attention. We intend to support the bill. It is now ten minutes to six o'clock, and in order that there may be a vote upon this measure I am delighted to sit down.

speechtext:
That was a slip of the tongue. I have misgivings about this measure because it would not be limited to merely agricultural

products; it would apply to lumber products, gravel, stone, sea products and so on. First of all, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill is to give the original producer the right of recovery from a bankrupt processor or person holding his goods, plus the costs of any improvements that may have been incurred in connection with the goods. However, there is already established in other areas legislation which grants priorities above those which now rank as even preferred claims. We have first of all-and this is something which must be considered-deductions for income tax that have been made from the pay of employees of a processor. This is a debt due to the crown, and it is clearly indicated in the Bankruptcy Act that this is a prior claim.
Second, and this also applies to the employees of such processors, there are the deductions that the processors have made from the pay of the employee and contributions which are due from the employer with respect to unemployment insurance. This also is a prior claim. Then in various provincial jurisdictions, for instance Alberta, we have what is called the exemptions act. This provides a protection to the individual; he is not thrown out on the street with only the clothes he is wearing. Not that this amounts to a debtor's paradise, but it allows every debtor a minimum. I am questioning whether such legislation as this will take precedence over these exemptions. I have not had an opportunity to consider all the points at which the purpose of this bill might run foul of other claims-for instance unpaid sales tax to the crown, and other prior claims established by statutes of this parliament as having precedence over ordinary claims.

speechtext:
That is certainly a point, but I submit that in giving second reading to a bill we are accepting the principle which it embodies, and the principle of this bill is to give priority to the claims of the producers of these goods. On the other hand, if many other claims are to rate above them, the principle of the bill may, in effect, be wrong. However, it is not my intention to talk this out. No one has raised these points so far, yet they go to the root of the priority which the sponsor of this bill is trying to set up.
Bankruptcy Act
This measure attempts to give to a particular class of creditors a priority which, I submit, may not be possible because of other legislation which may override it. Take, for example, the Unemployment Insurance Act or the Income Tax Act. Here, it is said: "Notwithstanding the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act-" and so on, certain claims will have prior effect. Thus, right away, there is conflict. The bill uses the words "in any other statute". There is a conflict of principles right there. I wish to draw these points to the attention of the house.
From another point of view I am wondering what adverse effect these proposals may have on small operators, small businessmen who wish to obtain a line of credit. The bill tries to protect one class in the economy. What will be the effect on another class? I have in mind a banker, or any other person who is granting credit, for example a wholesale lumber broker who grants credit to a lumber yard. Such a person may say to certain of their clients in the future because of this bill: "We are not going to give you any credit". The same position would apply in the agriculture industry. This is one of the difficulties which I envisage if we create a preferred class among creditors. When money is lent to certain types of producers, labor is granted certain safeguards or protection is afforded by section 88 of the Bank Act designed to encourage the granting of credit in respect of certain risky types of development; those are types of exemptions to the general principle that all creditors should share and share alike when somebody, unfortunately, goes bankrupt.
These are the points which worry me as far as the principle of this bill is concerned and, personally, I should like to see more answers furnished even before we accept the principle.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to recapitulate the various matters I have brought before the house so far excepting in so far as the decision of the NATO council is concerned endorsing a NATO nuclear strike force. I would simply say in that connection that the consensus is that that pool will not in a military sense have the slightest effect on the defence of Europe, to use the expression of an outstanding newspaper correspondent.
Today we live in a period when many people are led to a false sense of security brought about, no doubt in large measure, by the inaction of the Kremlin in the last six months or so in respect of those areas which were difficult and tender spots internationally-Berlin, Laos, and elsewhere. However, it cannot be repeated too often that periods of inaction or paralysis, as it were, on the part of the U.S.S.R. are in no way indicative of a change of destination or a detour along their desired road of ultimate world domination. It is very apparent that changes are taking place in the U.S.S.R. in circles which would lead one to believe that difficulties are being experienced in the Kremlin, that there are cracks and crevices between the various strata of the Kremlin. The trial and death sentence of Oleg Pankovsky, one of Russia's war heroes, a man occupying a fairly high position in the hierarchy, would indicate that all is not unity or solidarity within the Kremlin.
It is also significant that during this interregnum, as it were, between crisis and crisis the U.S.S.R. has made no forward step toward the acceptance of control in the matter of testing. Indeed, I think Britain and the United States have gone a long way towards an accommodation but have been unsuccessful in securing agreement, and unless this first step toward disarmament is secured the future is fraught with greater fears than ever before. Only last Saturday it was stated that at this time the air is filled with radioactive poison to an extent that has not been


so for a period of over a year. Unless some agreement is arrived at in connection with testing within the next four months, the general contemplation is that there will be a resumption of testing by the U.S.S.R. which, in turn, will result in a demanded resumption on the part of other nations. While I realize that summit conferences are not always effective, I do believe that at this time, during this period of the unfreezing of the cold war, something might well be achieved by the representatives of the "big three" as well as with other representatives of the various NATO countries, meeting with Khrushchev if possible, and also with representatives of countries under his domination. Unless something is done toward the achievement of this first step to world disarmament and the lessening of tensions, there may well be a hardening of the attitude of the U.S.S.R., since nothing effective has been done during a period of calm, and the fact that communist China continues to press the U.S.S.R. to more aggressive measures. That being so, all of us are in agreement that the strength of NATO must be maintained. The power to exercise retaliation in the event of any attack against the western world must be preserved.
In so far as what was done at the NATO conference is concerned, the setting up of an unnamed force with an unnamed objective is not an effective move in any sense of the word. Indeed, from an examination of the views of world leaders in public thinking, I found no one who expressed other than regret that more forward-looking action had not been taken by the NATO ministerial conference when it had the opportunity to do so.
With regard to matters which are under discussion today, and to which the Prime Minister made reference in answer to a question by myself, the setting up of a NATO sea-borne nuclear strategic force, Mr. Merchant is here. He has had talks today with the Prime Minister and various other ministers. A press report sets out in some detail what the plan is, which, of course, all of us know. The force would comprise 25 surface ships carrying a total of 200 long-range Polaris missiles. The ships would use mainly Atlantic ports in Europe and North America and possibly some on the great lakes.
What is the attitude of Canada to be to this? If I understood the Prime Minister correctly today, he indicated in his answer that no final decision would be made in this regard until the fullest of discussions had taken place in the defence committee. At the same time that the representative from Washington is here, Admiral Ricketts is in the United Kingdom, and certainly the general reaction to this force in the United Kingdom has not

been favourable. Viscount Montgomery, with that outspoken assurance that is always his, brushed it aside as completely unworthy of consideration. His description was that it was poppycock.
However, it is being considered over there as it is being considered here, and I think we are entitled to know something of the terms that are suggested by the United States. This was one of the propositions that were placed before the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom in Nassau. It brought about a change in Britain's defence technique. Britain gave up the Skybolt, something that she had built her hopes on, something that had been arranged by agreement between the United States and her, and substituted therefor was this multilateral nuclear force idea.
The first idea was that the Polaris missiles would be mounted on submarines and that these would be multicrewed submarines. That had its difficulties because if you had five or six nationalities represented in the crew of a submarine submerged for a period of 20 or 30 days you would have disagreements which would border on very serious difficulties, to say the least.
Then the question arose whether ships might be used. I think we are entitled to know something about this matter. I know that the Prime Minister made the statement recently that he was able to speak with greater authority on what should be done in foreign affairs when he was leader of the opposition than he was now as Prime Minister. When he was leader of the opposition he secured most of his information from the press; but now with the daily reports before him the assurance that he previously had had been considerably diminished.
However, throughout the western world there have been suggestions as to the terms of the plan. We in this house have had no information in that connection. The general consensus seems to be that the cost of this new force will be $400 million, that in so far as Britain is concerned she will make her contribution partly in warheads and in port facilities, and to a lesser degree in money. There has been a suggested division of control and financial responsibility. We in this house should know that. We should not have depend upon the usual well informed sources giving their opinions through the press. The consensus seems to be that the United States will put up 33 per cent of the cost, Britain 10 per cent and Canada 10 per cent.
When I suggested this afternoon that the cost to Canada would be some $40 to $50 million the Prime Minister said that whatever the cost might be it might not increase the amount of Canada's actual expenditure because there might be savings in other types of

Appointment of Defence Committee defence. The reason for this division of cost is in part to assure that the United States, Britain and Canada will have actual majority control through financial responsibility over this new body. It has been agreed that no nation will pay more than 40 per cent of the cost. It is hoped West Germany will contribute 33 per cent. This matter was discussed by the Prime Minister with the President of the United States during the visit to Hyannis Port and since then the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) has indicated that he has sought further information over and above that which was vouchsafed to the Prime Minister on that occasion.
Then I should like to find out, and I think the house has a right to know, what changes are contemplated in the McMahon act. Since 1947 or 1948, indeed, since the end of the second world war, the United States has exercised a control over atomic energy which until recently had not been subject to any suggestion of change. However, the McMahon act as it now stands prevents the giving of nuclear warheads and information to any country except Britain. What is the intention of the United States in this regard? Is legislation going to be brought in to amend that act before this new nuclear mixmaster crew plan is set up? The information I have is that the treaty will be ready for the senate of the United States at the beginning of next year.
These are things that we would like to know. Canada has become involved first of all in providing this tremendous power to NATO through our air force Starfighters, actually an aggressive nuclear force far and beyond what is contemplated by the expression "defensive weapons", and in addition is now contemplating entering into this field of a nuclear mixmaster force. We want to know something about this in the House of Commons.
The matter of security does not enter into the picture at all because these matters are being discussed publicly, and I feel that the Prime Minister when he concludes the debate might well place before the house and the country something of the general plan that the United States has in mind and which, through Mr. Merchant, has been brought fully to the knowledge and cognizance of the Canadian government.
Reverting for a moment to what I said regarding the Starfighters, they will now be adopted into the multilateral force. That force will not increase the military power of NATO. It will simply assure that the United States will still keep its finger on the control with the 14 other NATO countries having their fingers on the safety catch. But there is

Appointment of Defence Committee something more. It is expected as well that other NATO members will provide a greater share of the cost. In that connection I do not see why Canada should be required to pay more and to make a greater contribution to NATO and to the defence of freedom than it has. We in this country have not failed to do our part and no other country in NATO, with the possible exception of the United States, has contributed as much as Canada has in proportion to population. This has been so throughout the period of NATO. Why, now, should it be considered that Canada should contribute even a greater share in consequence of the acceptance of that plan? I am not going into the particulars tonight of Canada's contribution, but I think it is generally accepted that no country has contributed more than have we, in proportion, measured on the basis of population.
Then, I should like to know from the Prime Minister about NORAD, the North American defence. Has the United States sought permission, since the present government has come into office, to store air to air missiles in Canada on its leased bases? If so, are negotiations going on at this time to provide for such storage within our country? In that regard I will say immediately that I am not asking for particulars, for in doing so I might intrude upon the field of security. However, I do believe that the Canadian people have a right to know what changes, if any, have taken place since April 22 in this connection in relation to the United States. We never had any disagreement until the famed press release was issued by the department of state on January 30. Throughout the entire period of time our relations were always the relations of good neighbours.
I suggest that we have the right to know whether or not these comings and goings back and forth between Ottawa and Washington that have been intensified in recent weeks represent any increased responsibilities or constitute the acceptance of additional responsibilities by Canada in connection with defence.
Then, as I said in the beginning of my remarks, this afternoon's statement made by the Prime Minister, in answer to a question of mine, to the effect that the present government was most interested in assuring that Canada's responsibilities in the conventional field should be increased, and the corollary would be that our nuclear contribution would thereby be diminished, was not a loose answer given on the spur of the moment. It represented something about which I believe we are entitled to information. What is the changing technique or relationship? What attitude is the Canadian government taking? What will its stand be with the other nations of


NATO as those nations meet together from time to time within the next year or two to determine the defence possibilities and potentialities of NATO?
All of these things are matters that deserve attention and upon which parliament is entitled to information. I look forward to the meetings of the committee, which we intend to support. We intend to support this resolution. We hope that out of the committee will come extensive information. We hope that the committee will not be translated into a kind of search and snoop committee, the purpose of which will be to look into the past. We hope that it will have the attitude of looking into the future and, as Canadians in that committee, primarily as Canadians and not as party representatives, the members of that committee will endeavour to bring about the recommendations which, while not binding upon the government in any way, will constitute a consensus of viewpoints that should be truly representative of all parts of Canada.
However, in saying that I cannot understand why, following the undertaking and promise made at Kingston by the Prime Minister that the whole defence situation was going to be looked at, and his further declaration that we should endeavour to take defence out of politics, this government, without consulting parliament in any way, made the determination it did prior to the meeting of NATO, and confirmed in the NATO meeting, to arm our air force overseas with offensive weapons.

Mr. Speaker, it does seem, judging by the speeches which have been made, that this debate on the creation of a national defence committee has ranged far and wide.
What little knowledge I have about the rules of this house led me to believe that we had to hold closely to the establishment of that committee. But because hon. members were allowed to wander away a bit from the subject, we have had to listen to rather lengthy speeches.
The motion speaks of a committee appointed to report from time to time its observations and opinions.
I am wondering what purpose will be served if, from time to time, the committee airs views or makes representations when the policy of the government has already been enunciated. The committee will be unable to change the government's decisions.
Even the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) said so, as indicated in Hansard of May 30:

It would certainly be no substitute for the responsibility which the government must have in the making of decisions in regard to defence, the same responsibility which it has in making decisions on other aspects of policy.
And a little farther:
No government can evade its responsibilities in the matter of defence or in any other field by the establishment of a committee.
Of course, fact-finding committees can always be interesting.
However, when it is known that several members will be kept busy, that many witnesses will be called before the committee- and it was also announced that several trips will perhaps be necessary to visit the military establishments under the jurisdiction either of Canada herself or of NATO or other organizations-it is realized that expenses will be relatively high and that the decisions of the committee will have no effect at all.
In order not to take too much time I would like to say a few words about what should be the set-up of the defence committee which, during the election campaign, was advocated by a party other than the Liberal party. I am sure others will share my views.
By the way, I would like to give a few explanations to the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) who is wondering how a committee can be non-partisan if it is made up of members of a party. A committee can be made up of members of a party who, for once, will act not so much as supporters of that party but as members representing the will or wishes of the people of their riding, that is their electors. It is very easy to have a non-partisan committee even if it is made up of members who belong to one party or another.
I would suggest that the information given and the recommendations made by the committee be provided to the house and that members be given the opportunity to vote not as members of a party but individually, freely, without partisanship, according to their own feelings about the recommendations of the defence committee but especially according to the opinions of their constituents.
The more we go the more we find that nuclear arms are a complex question. Many are those who have preconceived ideas without knowing what this is all about. However, I feel that we should consider the opinions of our constituents, and that is why I recommend-I doubt that this will be accepted- that the report of the defence committee be submitted to the house and that members of all parties be allowed to vote freely, that
Appointment of Defence Committee is not necessarily along party lines, so that the people of Canada may be truly represented here on this question, whatever the policy of the different parties.
I for one know many members who do not agree with the official policy of their own party.
So, if Canada is truly a democracy, if our election to this house was truly democratic, I believe that for once the House of Commons should give an example of democracy in action by allowing its members to truly represent their constituents here.

Mr. Deputy Speaker, this is the first time I have had the opportunity of participating in debate in the twenty sixth parliament and I would like to avail myself of the opportunity to congratulate the Speaker and yourself on your election to the very high offices you hold. I think all of us are quite sure that both His Honour the Speaker and yourself will carry out your duties in the highest traditions of the house.
The first time that any of us heard very much about this Commons defence committee was through reading a Canadian Press report during the recent election campaign. That report attributes to the Prime Minister the statement that a Liberal government would set up an all-party House of Commons defence committee right away, to take the defence issue away from partisan polities, and that the committee's work would be part of a Liberal government's review of Canadian defence policies to determine an appropriate role for this country. This statement was reported to have been made by the Prime Minister in Kingston, Ontario, on March 26 last.
The clear inference of this statement was first of all that any such committee would be non-partisan; second, that such a committee would provide a review of defence policies for the purposes of determining Canada's role in defence. Now, this seemed very good. At least it was good election bait, but a number of us who have spent some time in the house and who are familiar with the operations of the committees of the house were a little dubious about the practicality of such a suggestion. However, being fair-minded persons, we decided to wait and see what would transpire.
Well, Mr. Speaker, now things have changed. We now have the terms of reference of the committee and we find there are to be 24 members allotted as follows: 12 Liberal members, eight members of the official opposition and two each from the other two parties in the house. Presumably the chairman will

Appointment of Defence Committee be elected from among the government members and of course he will have an extra vote in case of any ties. That, Mr. Speaker, deals very decisively with the non-partisan aspect of such a committee because any recommendations coming from it would clearly be the views of the government members on the committee.
Subsequently during this debate, if I heard him correctly, the Minister of National Defence informed us that there would be no classified information provided to the committee. One can only conclude from that that there would be no information of any real value provided to the committee, and I for one would like to know how defence policies, even in fairly general terms, could be recommended without having any knowledge or any facts of real importance?
It is quite true that, similar to the external affairs committee which has been sitting for a number of years, and of which I have been a member on various occasions, committee members can make general observations and recommendations; but without classified information it is impossible to make any real recommendations of importance. In any event, how could such a committee, even if provided with classified information, recommend any sort of policies, even in general terms, or indeed study expenditures, unless the committee knew the purposes for which our armed forces are to be used?
To know these purposes we have to have some comprehensive idea of the government's foreign policy. In essence the armed services are only the instruments for carrying out certain aspects of our foreign policy, which of course includes national defence. Defence and foreign policy are like the two blades of a scissors, one has very little purpose without the other. The committee that has been proposed cannot recommend defence policy, or even determine our appropriate role, without very great detailed knowledge of our foreign policy, and in view of this I am very surprised we have not heard from the Secretary of State for External Affairs in this debate.
I am also surprised that we have not heard from the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin) who in days gone by, if my memory serves me correctly, was a parliamentary assistant to the secretary of state for external affairs, and who has a great and wide knowledge of this subject. In other words, to have some knowledge of what our foreign policy must be in order to determine our defence role, I would hope the committee would call as witnesses the Secretary of State for External Affairs and some of his senior officials. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I go a great
[Mr. Nesbitt.!
deal further than that. In order for this committee to be effective I think the committee on external affairs, when it is set up, should hold joint meetings with the defence committee; or better still, the two committees might meet continually. I cannot understand how defence policies can be determined without a very extensive knowledge of the foreign policies of the present government. I think that only by one or other of the methods I have suggested can this be accomplished. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, there should be either occasional joint meetings of the external affairs committee and the proposed defence committee, or the two committees should meet jointly and continually or, at the very least, senior officials of the Department of External Affairs and, of course, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) should be called as witnesses.
It may be a platitude to say that we know foreign policy and defence policy are very closely allied; but just for a moment, and very briefly, I would like to illustrate how our foreign policy is in fact so closely related to our defence policy and what sort of questions the committee should consider in this regard. It is often said that our foreign policy comprises our relationships with NATO, with the United Nations, with the commonwealth and our special relationships with the United States of America and other countries. But the first four of these are of course the most important. So far in this debate our relationships with NATO and the United States of America have formed the chief considerations in discussing the relationship between our defence and foreign policies. However, for a moment or two I would like to consider the relationship between foreign and defence policies with respect to our commonwealth and United Nations relationships. As far as our commonwealth relationships are concerned, defence policy is a very important thing. The previous government and, I understand, the present government recently provided military aid to India to help her with her difficulties with communist China. This sort of situation may arise with respect to other countries in the commonwealth, and certainly this committee should make some recommendation to the government in this regard. I would like to leave that phase of the subject with those remarks.
Now we come to our relationships with the United Nations. I think one might divide these into three headings. First, our special forces; second, nuclear policy, and third disarmament. With respect to the special forces, Canada in the past has with great distinction contributed forces to the Near East to serve on the border between Israel and Egypt. As I understand it, there has been very little difficulty in this

regard and our efforts have been very successful and very commendable. In more recent times we have provided communications troops to the Congo. These special forces certainly require special training in geography, specialized warfare such as jungle and desert warfare and the like. In addition to that, special knowledge of the customs and habits of the people of the area to which they are sent is very essential.
For a good many meetings I happened to be a representative of this country in the United Nations Congo advisory committee. While I cannot, of course, go into detail as to what transpired in that committee, I can say from what I heard that every nation which provided troops to the Congo would have gotten into much less difficulty had those troops been provided with some specialized knowledge and training of the geography, habits and customs of the people. Indeed I think I can go as far as saying that some of the difficulties our troops suffered were due to certain misunderstandings. I think if we are to send troops to help the United Nations if such occasions arise in the future, this committee could well consider looking into the matter of providing special training for those troops. I might even go as far as suggesting that perhaps some special adviser who has a knowledge of the area concerned should be provided for the troops when they go to these areas.
Then we come to the question of nuclear policy. This is a very important aspect of our foreign policy at the United Nations. The former government had two policies in this regard. First of all, that there should be no nuclear testing; they were opposed to nuclear testing of any sort. On the occasion when I had the honour of representing this country at the United Nations, the government of the day was opposed to the spread of nuclear weapons as long as there appeared to be some reasonable prospect of disarmament. That was the second policy.
Of course, I do not know what the policies of the present government are in this respect. If the policy is there, it seems a little doubtful, a little hard to find at the moment. But if these policies are to be changed, this committee should know what the changes are in order to be able to make appropriate recommendations. In this field it has been the stand of the present government, as I understand it, that our Bomarcs, CF-lOl's and 104G's are to be provided with some sort of nuclear weapons. That may be all very well, but I would like to point out in this regard, Mr. Speaker, that during recent years and dating back to the period when the Liberal government was previously in office, Canada had acquired a very favourable reputation at the

We acquired a great deal of prestige in that regard, I might say. More than that-and a great deal of the credit in this instance goes to the hon. gentleman who is now the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson)-over the years we have acquired a reputation in the United Nations for being an independent country with independent and constructive suggestions to offer.
If we acquire nuclear weapons under the conditions as outlined by the government, we are going to have to forgo a great deal of this prestige at the United Nations. Even latterly, when the new Asian and African countries came into the United Nations a couple of years ago they said to me, "Ah well, Canada is really a satellite of the United States". If we acquire these weapons under the conditions which have been prescribed, this is a danger we are going to have to run at the United Nations. If we expect our prestige to remain constant or to improve we have to take into consideration the effect which the acquisition of nuclear weapons, under the terms we have heard in this house, is going to have.
In addition to that there is the element of suspicion. A number of hon. members in this house have had occasion from time to time to deal with representatives of the Soviet union. I think anyone who has done that knows very well that representatives of the Soviet union are exceedingly suspicious. That is one of the problems that every country has in dealing with subjects such as disarmament, and so on. If Canada acquires nuclear weapons, even for defensive purposes, I am quite sure that the Soviet union will regard these weapons as being just about as much for defence as we regarded the rockets in Cuba for defence.
All these things have to be taken into consideration. We must consider whether it is worth while for Canada to acquire nuclear weapons. It may be that it is worth while for us to do so, and I think this is something on which the committee should make a recommendation. But in making such a recommendation it is important to bear in mind the weight on the other side of the scales. It may be essential for our defence that we should arm the Bomarcs, the CF-lOl's and so on; it is up to the committee to make recommendations to the government in this regard. On the other hand, it should be remembered that if we do take this step we shall lose our leadership in the United Nations in the field of disarmament; we shall arouse increased tension and suspicion between the Soviet union and the western world, and we shall run the risk of being

Appointment of Defence Committee increasingly regarded by the African and Asian nations as a military satellite of the United States, thus further weakening our position in the United Nations. I am not presuming to tell this house what the answer should be, but this is something we should all consider and a situation which the committee should bear in mind in malting its recommendations.
Disarmament is a field in which Canada has worked unceasingly for many years. When we consider what kinds of weapons we ought to have in the future-and the committee should certainly make some recommendations to the government in this regard-I hope General Burns, the distinguished soldier who has served Canada so well in so many fields and who is now our representative on the disarmament commission, will be called to give evidence. I say this because in formulating defence policy for the future it would be important to have General Burns' views as to the situation which might arise if any progress were made in disarmament.
These are some of the subjects which ought to be considered by the committee. Not all of us can expect to serve on this committee. I hope the recommendations made by so many hon. members of this house will be given the closest consideration by members of that body when it meets.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on this motion has ranged far and wide and the issues involved in setting up this committee have been well discussed. It is not my intention, therefore, to rehash any of the arguments which have been put forward, but there are one or two things which I feel should be said before the motion is passed and the committee is established.
The first thing I should like to say is something about which I feel very strongly, as a result of experiences over a number of days and weeks, and particularly as a result of what has happened in the last two days. Let me put it as succinctly as I can. I think that we, as members of the House of Commons, and the Canadian people whom we represent, are entitled to the facts-entitled to the truth about our defence situation. I want to pinpoint this argument by speaking with special reference to the so-called commitments which the previous government is supposed to have made.
I have been following this subject closely. I have been listening to what has been said. I have read what has been written. Yet I still do not know whether the previous government made any commitments, so far as acquiring nuclear arms is concerned. In this House of Commons we are expected to speak

responsibly. When an hon. member makes a statement we are expected to take that statement at its face value. That is true of all of us. But somehow it seems to apply with particular force to those hon. members who are members of the privy council. We who are ordinary members of this house are faced with this situation: we have heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), the former prime minister, declare categorically that no commitments were made by the former government. We have heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the present government (Mr. Martin) tell us they have ascertained that commitments were made. I have read and re-read the statements made by each of these two hon. gentlemen. Each used words which were most explicit. But where does it leave us? If it leaves us not knowing what the truth is, where does it leave the Canadian people?
I feel one of the things which this committee must do is to ascertain the truth- whether there was, or was not, any commitment made by the previous government for Canada to acquire nuclear weapons. I recognize that the past is past. Perhaps the present and the future are of greater concern. But I do not see how we can carry on the democratic and parliamentary processes if, with respect to a factual item as basic as this one, we cannot get the truth.
Because I have said that two hon. gentlemen in particular have made contrary statements, let me put them on record. The Leader of the Opposition, speaking in this house on May 21 as reported on page 126 of Hansard said this:
I say immediately that there are and were no commitments on the part of Canada to accept nuclear weapons. And, Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt that since taking office hon. gentlemen opposite, busy as they are in these days of decision, have searched with microscopic care. They have searched but they have not found.
Today, the Leader of the Opposition repeated that sentiment when he said-and in this instance I am relying on my own notes which I took at the time-that the present government had snooped and searched and sought but had found nothing. I cannot imagine a member of the House of Commons being more precise, more definite, than the Leader of the Opposition has been. He says the government of which he was the head made no commitment for Canada to acquire nuclear arms and he says that the government now in office has had time to snoop and search and seek, but that it has not been able to find any commitment.
On the other hand, the other day, in reply to a question on the order paper filed by my hon. friend the member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) to be found in Hansard of June

5 on page 675, the Secretary of State for External Affairs had something to say on this subject. The question was in two main parts. This was part one:
Has the government of Canada found out whether its predecessor entered into any commitment or undertaking with NATO or any government or person involving the use by Canadian forces of nuclear warheads in Europe or in Canada?
The answer given to that question by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as it appears in Hansard, was in one word. That word is, "Yes". So where are we? There is a categorical statement by the Leader of the Opposition that there were no commitments by the previous government, and there is an equally categorical statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the present government has found those commitments. We in this house and the people of Canada are entitled to the truth. I hope this committee, when it is established, will recognize that is one of its responsibilities, to go at this until it has ascertained what the facts are.
I am further confused in all this, as I am sure most hon. members are, by what happened yesterday. I presented a motion which I had hoped would clear up this confusion. It was a motion for production of papers in which I asked that any documents citing these commitments be produced. In the midst of that discussion the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) said that there were no documents to produce. His exact words are to be found on page 688 of Hansard, where he is reported as saying:

There are none such to produce.
I was a little confused when a few minutes later the Leader of the Opposition voted against a motion to produce a summary of the documents which he said do not exist. That puzzled me, but perhaps I can understand his position. He said that we should have the documents in their entirety or nothing at all. I took it from his other categorical statement that there were no documents which contain any commitments; and from the other side of the house we are told in the simplest and most straightforward of terms, yes, there are commitments which were made by the previous government which this government, having got into office, has found.
Mr. Speaker, the question which my colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood, placed on the order paper, and which was answered yesterday at page 675 of Hansard, had a second part to it, as a natural development. First of all he asked whether any of these commitments had been found, and the answer was yes. The second part of the question was as follows:

If so (a) to whom was the commitment or undertaking given (b) what were the terms of such commitment or undertaking (c) was the undertaking explicitly or by implication revocable by the government and under what conditions (d) was the commitment or undertaking in writing and what was the nature of the document (e) by whom was it given or made, and with what authority (f) what was the date of such commitment, if any, or the ratification thereof by the former government of Canada?
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if the answer "Yes" is correct, and if the present government by snooping, searching and seeking has found that there were commitments, here was the opportunity, in answer to the second question by the hon. member for Greenwood, to give enough factual information to prove the statement that this government had found the former government's commitments.

That was a pretty strong interjection from my hon. friend the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. I confess that when I first put my motion on the order paper I thought it would prove that either one side or the other was telling the truth, but as this situation has developed I have got lost. He repeated it tonight. He said they had snooped, searched and sought but found nothing. But the government says it has found something.
The present government was given a clear opportunity in the question of my colleague to fortify its answer. There are several paragraphs to the answer and I would ask the house to listen to part of it, as reported on page 675 of Hansard:
In respect of Canadian forces in Europe the undertakings arise out of NATO processes. NATO does not enter into formal agreements or treaties with member nations regarding their military contributions. The military authorities of the alliance set certain requirements and individual countries determine what contributions they will make toward meeting those requirements. The whole process is accomplished by direct discussions with the NATO commanders concerned and is confirmed in an annual review process which is secret.
Well, I hope somebody understands that. I hope somebody can assess that paragraph and tell me whether the government has found the commitment, as it says it has, or whether it is just shoehorning us into the position of becoming a nuclear power.

speechtext:
-because the answer given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) is referring to what took place when the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and his colleagues formed the government, when these processes which the present government says are the means by which we have become a potential nuclear power were begun.
I want now to move from the point which I think I have established, namely that we are in a state of confusion, that we do not know who to believe, that we do not know what the facts are and what the truth is. Surely, the committee should get this for us. I want to move on to this statement, that if we are becoming a nuclear power, either big, middle-sized or small, surely this is the most striking, most significant, most important change ever to take place in Canadian defence policy. If that is the case, it is a change which we in this party do not want to see take place. But it is taking place. Therefore it should surely be done out in the open in a forthright manner, and not just because the processes in which we have become involved somehow shoehorn us into the nuclear club and take us into it by a back door method. This is too important and significant a development in Canadian defence history for it to happen in this way.
Mr. Speaker, look at what has happened. We have a government in power today whose members a few months ago were opposed to nuclear weapons for Canada. On January 12 this year that position changed. We were told the reason the Liberal party changed its policy was because it had discovered that the previous government had made commitments. We cannot find out whether or not

that is true, and I think we know less about it today than at any time in the piece. We discover, from the kind of answer given to my colleague from Greenwood yesterday and from what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said in rely to my motion yesterday, as reported at page 688, that we are being taken down the path into the position of being a nuclear power, not by an overt decision of the kind which can be put on a table and told about in precise terms, but because of some processes which get going which we cannot stop. It is like the automatic elevators we have in this building. If somebody puts his finger on the button it has got to go through the process. Somewhere somebody is putting his finger on something and we are being taken down the path and one of these days we will find ourselves part of the nuclear club, a nuclear power of some sort or other, without the matter ever having been discussed in an open way and on a forthright basis.
Yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), in his comments on the motion that I put which I hoped would clear up the matter, did not say categorically at that point that there were commitments as he did in answer to the order paper question of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), but he implied that there were commitments because he said:
The commitments entered into by the government of Canada to accept nuclear weapons for Canadian forces in NATO and at home are to be found, inter alia-
You always fool somebody when you put in a Latin phrase.
-in Canadian submissions under the NATO annual review procedure, in statements made in the Canada-United States ministerial committee on joint defence, and in the records of the discussions in the permanent joint board on defence. These documents include information the release of which could prejudice the national security of Canada and of its allies.
If that is where these commitments are, Mr. Speaker, surely the sentences that were precise and definite and that did commit us could be extracted and could be given to us. Here we are in the position that there is being made for us the most important, the most significant, the most far reaching decision in defence policy that has ever been made for this country and we cannot get the truth about it. We cannot find the date on which it was made, we cannot find the terms, we cannot get the document, we cannot get any evidence, any proof of it whatsoever.

speechtext:
As my leader has pointed out, parliament has had no chance to commit

the country on this matter either under the previous government or under this one.
We support the proposition that a defence committee should be established. In fact, the more this kind of thing comes to light the more it looks to me as though this should be a permanent committee, not just a committee for this session to review this particular issue. It looks to me that if we are going to have defence policy put over on us in this way through the back door, by the shoehorn method, we have got to have a permanent defence committee of the House of Commons to keep its eye on what is happening.
I hope, therefore, that in this committee there will be no restrictions. If it is necessary for it to meet in camera to get the facts and the documents in order to straighten out some of these things, let it meet in camera, but I think we in the House of Commons as a whole have a right to expect from that defence committee a clearcut report in which it tells us what the truth is. Were there commitments? Were there not? Were there commitments made by the previous government or is the present government making commitments for Canada relying on the statement that the previous government had made them? The situation is as confused as it can possibly be. Surely in a field that may well determine life and death for the human race these matters should be dealt with in a forthright and open manner.
This is a democratic parliament in which we are dealing with these things. It is not good enough for us to be caught in the position where the Leader of the Opposition says one thing and the Secretary of State for External Affairs say the very opposite and we are called upon to accept both of them as being truthful and honourable men. What do we know when we come to the question of how we got over this line from being a conventional military power to a nuclear military power? We cannot be told, no matter how precisely the question is put. We cannot be told what the date was, what the document was, what the commitment was.
This is not good enough, Mr. Speaker. This is why we support the establishing of this committee and we earnestly hope that it will be given all of the opportunities, all of the rights and privileges, that pertain to committees so that it can get the answers, so that it can bring this business out in the open, so that we can know what our defence policy is and where we go from here.
Our position in this corner of the house is well known. We think that Canada should not acquire nuclear weapons. We regret the decisions made in this direction already but whatever decision is taken surely it should
Appointment of Defence Committee be taken in a parliamentary way with all the facts being made known to us and, above all, let us have for parliament, let us have for the people of Canada, the truth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group welcome the announcement as well as the resolution calling for the setting up of a defence committee. Hon. members will recall that the leader of this group, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), requested some time ago that a committee be set up that would, in the light of all relevant information and factors, make recommendations with respect to a defence policy adequate for the defence of this nation. After two of our members had spoken in this debate outlining our position we intended to rest our case, but because the debate has continued for a considerable length of time we have decided that we will risk the displeasure of those who would like to conclude the debate and once more participate on this occasion.

Appointment of Defence Committee
We believe that national defence is too vital an issue to remain a political football and this is what it has been for a considerable length of time. We believe that a committee such as is proposed can do a very worth-while job in looking into the entire defence picture, assessing the situation with respect to our defence role and then coming forward with the suggestions and recommendations that the committee believes will be in the best interests of the Canadian nation.
I know that the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) spoke in rather sceptical fashion regarding this committee and suggested that we were rather naive in expecting that anything worth while would be achieved by the operations of such a committee. However, we believe that this committee, if given the chance, if given the opportunity, can come forward with some very worth-while proposals regarding the issues involved. I should like to make my remarks as brief as possible but I wish to suggest some of the factors which should be considered by this committee when it is in session. First of all, I believe it should somehow or other try to establish the nature of the challenge before us in Canada and in the free world. Sometimes we forget the objective, sometimes we forget the challenge and because we forget the challenge that is before us we kind of shoot off in all directions, when we try to establish some way in which we can meet that challenge and solve our problem.
We have heard a great deal down through the past number of years about the strategy of world communism. It has been outlined not only in military terms, but on many occasions it has been pointed out that it is more or less an ideological attack. I think this is true. We have not heard so much recently about the struggle for men's minds. I am sure, however, we all realize that that struggle is still continuing, that battle is still in progress. I wonder whether or not this committee is going to just consider the whole issue on the basis of military consideration or whether they are going to have the opportunity to consider it from the other angles, the ideological aspects of the challenge, the economic aspects of the challenge, as well as the military.
Now, I do not think it is necessary for the house at the present time to discuss at length the type of armaments required and these various matters. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that should be the responsibility of the committee. I think it would save a great deal of time if it were left to that body. I would suggest, however, that the committee should give consideration to the nature of the challenge

before us and then try to come forward with some positive suggestion as to how to meet that challenge.
The second matter to which I should like to refer is one that was dealt with very fully and adequately by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Since he has dealt with it so fully, I am just going to refer to it at the moment. I believe that the committee must, somehow or other, determine as to whether or not commitments have been made in respect of nuclear armaments. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has referred to the conflicting statements made by the Leader of the Opposition and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Perhaps we could tie the Prime Minister into that situation, because we find that at the present time on the government side we have the statement that commitments have been made and the present government is only fulfilling the commitments as they proceed to acquire nuclear weapons. On the other hand, we have the assertion that no commitments have been made. We find, therefore, that we are betwixt and between. It is very difficult, as has been pointed out, to find out just what the situation is.
I would suggest that these right hon. gentlemen stop talking in riddles, that they come right out and say what they mean and prove their points. Then, we in the House of Commons as well as the people at large will be able to understand the situation in a clearer fashion. So long as these gentlemen talk around in circles and in riddles, I am afraid the situation is not going to be clarified to the satisfaction of either the house or the people of the country as a whole.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the third consideration that should occupy the attention of this committee should be the nature of the contribution we can make in our own defence and the fulfilment of our obligations to the other nations of the world. On other occasions the leader of this group has pointed out very clearly what we believe would be an adequate and sane defence policy for Canada. We have suggested that we believe at the present time, so far as we can assess the situation, Canada can make its greatest contribution in fields other than the nuclear field. We have emphasized time and time again that we could make our greatest contribution in the field of conventional arms, detection and communication, and in the other phases that do not require actual entry into the nuclear situation.
But once again we find that this proposal has not apparently met with the approval of the Prime Minister or the members of his government. Some time ago we debated a subamendment in respect of nuclear arms.

Somehow or other the idea got across the country that this was a straight vote on whether or not to accept nuclear weapons for Canada's forces. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that a vote against that subamendment did not constitute a vote for nuclear weapons. We all recognize the fact that it was a want of confidence motion. I believe that to read anything else into it is just a little less than honest.
We would suggest, therefore, that this committee should study very carefully the nature of the contribution that we can best make, and find out whether or not we can make it perhaps as I have said in fields other than the nuclear field. We think of our financial situation. We consider the continual increase in our national debt. We think of the difficult economic situation through which we have recently passed and we ask ourselves the question, are we in a position to assume responsibility, from a financial point of view, for the acquisition of nuclear weapons and the maintenance that this would involve? We also think of our nation as a great nation. Geographically, it is a great nation, and so far as quality is concerned. We also recognize the fact that we have just a little less than 19 million people, and when we consider the problem from this point of view, we suggest that possibly our contribution should be in fields that are not perhaps as onerous, but yet as needful, as the entry into the nuclear field.
Now we have the Prime Minister stating on a number of occasions that the government is going to fulfil the commitments that Canada has made, and then renegotiate our position with a view, somehow or other, to finding a non-nuclear role for the Canadian forces. I would suggest we have not heard much about that recently. It has somehow been forgotten and instead of searching out another field and another role for Canadian forces, it seems as though we are rushing headlong into the nuclear field without any intention whatever of stopping.
There is another matter that I believe should be considered, and it is this: This committee should consider how we can best achieve this higher goal of peace and security that every Canadian, I believe, desires our nation should achieve. We have mentioned the astronomical amounts that are being spent by Canada on defence, or at least we have inferred that. Then, we are reminded by reports in the newspapers today that perhaps we will be saddled with additional expenses in regard to our military contribution. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we ought to give serious consideration to the means whereby we can achieve, as I have

Appointment of Defence Committee said, the higher goal of peace and security that constitutes the dream and aspiration of the Canadian people.
There have been discussions in the field of disarmament and I believe we all recognize that the governments of the past made valuable contributions in the quest for disarmament. I had an opportunity of being attached as an observer to the Canadian delegation to the United Nations several years ago, and I remember the activities of the delegation at that time as it endeavoured to accomplish something in the field of disarmament. I also followed with a great deal of interest and appreciation the activities of the former secretary of state for external affairs, the Hon. Mr. Green, as he sought in a very able and sincere manner to accomplish something in this particular field. We appreciate that, and today I believe the need is urgent, even more urgent than ever before in history, that every attempt and every endeavour be put forth to achieve some r easure of understanding with respect to disarmament, not only in so far as nuclear weapons are concerned but conventional weapons as well.
I believe the committee should consider the matter of assistance to other nations as a factor in the defence of our own nation, the defence of this continent and the defence of the free world, but above all I would suggest one of the greatest ways in which we can make a contribution in the defence of Canada is to make our nation strong economically, strong morally and, yes, strong militarily in order that we might present to the nations of the world an example of what can be done under a free, democratic and Christian way of life.
There are those who suggest in a rather sceptical, almost cynical manner, that this committee will just be a sop to silence the critics. I would not want to take that attitude. I do not intend to take it, but I would suggest that with the way the government has been moving forward in this particular field of defence it might almost develop into that, because in so many cases it seems as though the government is pressing forward rapidly, almost with indecent haste, in order to reach certain objectives before the committee has an opportunity of studying the matter and bringing it to the attention of the house.
Reference has been made to the discussions that are currently taking place with Mr. Merchant from the United States. It has been pointed out by the Prime Minister that these are more or less routine, and are the culmination of a series of discussions that have been taking place with the various NATO countries. I would point out we have had an assurance from the Prime Minister, and I

Appointment of Defence Committee believe we can depend on it, that before any move is made with respect to this type of force which goes beyond defence and constitutes an offensive force in many respects, it is something which should be brought before the committee and before the house for full discussion before action is taken.
The terms of the resolution indicate that the committee will present its observations and opinions, and the Prime Minister has also indicated that the committee will not have access to classified information. It almost seems as though he is pulling the teeth out of the committee before it starts its work. He is putting limitations upon it which will make it almost impossible for it to function adequately, and we only trust that in the area of classified information it will just be classified and not the type of information that perhaps the government does not wish, or does not think, the committee should have in its possession.
I also trust that the observations and opinions will not just be considered observations and opinions, but will be considered recommendations that are worthy of the careful consideration of the government, because we would like to think that every hon. member of the house, whether on the government or opposition side, is desirous of arriving at a policy that will be consistent with the standards of morality, and also be adequate for the defence of our nation. With these observations, Mr. Speaker, we would like to rest our case at this time and trust the committee will be set up and allowed to proceed with its work.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few brief remarks at this time. I notice of course that the Prime Minister is very anxious to stand up and close off the debate, but before he gets that opportunity I wish to say the substance of my few remarks is an appeal to an appropriate spokesman for the government, either the Prime Minister or the Minister of National Defence, to give this house and the people of Canada, at this time, a rather comprehensive statement on the position of the government with regard to the question of national defence, nuclear arms, our relations with NORAD and with NATO.
The reasons why I feel this is an appropriate time for such a statement are, first, that although the resolution is to set up a defence committee the Prime Minister, when he moved the resolution, confined his remarks to the question of whether or not the committee should be set up, and to what the terms of reference of the committee should be. But, subsequent to that by agreement, as stated

by the house leader, the debate on the resolution came to be of wide content on the whole field of national defence. Actually this is the tone of the speeches that have been made in the debate to date and, this having taken place, surely this is a time for a spokesman of the government to give the house and the public the statement I have suggested?
When the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) first spoke on this question he suggested that the Minister of National Defence might want to make a statement. At the time the minister declined. Subsequently that evening, a week ago today, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) again coaxed the minister to make a statement. The minister did but, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the contents of the statement he made further indicate the need for a different type of statement at this time, because what the minister said a week ago tonight indicated the complete lack of information that exists.
He did give us one or two little gems of information, one of course being that a survey during the last election showed 30 per cent of the people believed Bomarcs were intercontinental ballistic missiles. Then he went on to say:
-some of the facts and figures used in this debate are just about as absurd as that.
Surely that statement by the minister indicates that some further elucidation is required? The minister went on to say:
This is no reflection on anyone, but really only a demonstration of the fact that for the last three or four years the Canadian people and the Canadian parliament have been starved of real information on which they could base an intelligent opinion.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the starvation has now turned into a famine. The Minister of National Defence went on to say, in his statement in this debate:
Consequently I had to go outside this country in order to seek this information. I had to get the reports of the United States congressional committees and read them at length, where they told not only about the defence forces of the United States but gave much more information about Canadian forces than X could get from my own government.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, there is some compulsion on the Minister of National Defence to share this information with the ignorant members of this house, certainly those on this side of the chamber. I submit that this is a second reason for now being an appropriate time for the minister to make a comprehensive statement on this subject. I recognize that under the rules of the house the Minister of National Defence has made a statement in this debate, but I am quite sure that if he were to request unanimous consent

in order to make a further statement, all hon. members on this side of the chamber would give such consent.
Another reason for my thinking this is an appropriate time for the government to make a comprehensive statement is this. Although it is proposed to set up this committee, the fact of the matter is that from all the information I have been able to get from the press-very little in this house-a major decision as to defence has already been taken by the government, namely to accept nuclear arms on Canadian soil subject to an agreement with the United States, and to accept what might well be offensive weapons for our forces overseas. Surely if that decision has been taken by the government this house is now entitled to an explanation from the government as to the reasons which prompted them to make such a decision. Is the major reason the fact, as they maintain, that the previous government had committed Canada to accepting nuclear arms? We are entitled to know from the government what their position is. A further reason for my thinking the government should at this time make a comprehensive statement is the events of the last election. The question of defence and nuclear weapons was a major and important issue in the last election campaign. This government has been in power since April 22 and as yet we have had no statement of a comprehensive nature or of any substance from any member of the government on this important question. I should like to quote from an article in the Montreal Gazette of February 15 this year commenting on what the Prime Minister had said on this question, that he has "some ideas" of Canada's defence role in the future, and that he will make his views known in detail if the Liberals are elected.
Mr. Speaker, when, may I ask? Perhaps the Prime Minister or the Minister of National Defence, his spokesman, will tell us, if they are not prepared to make their views known at this time, when they will be prepared to do so. If the defence committee is set up, as I assume it will be, and sits, when will be the next occasion this house will have an opportunity to debate the question of national defence? As I see it, it may not be until the defence estimates are placed before the house and, judging by the hesitancy on the part of the government to deal with this question to date, I would hazard a guess that the defence estimates may be the last of the estimates to be placed before the house. So it may not be until late this year, or perhaps later than that, that the house will again have a formal opportunity to discuss national defence. Unless the Prime Minister or the Minister of
Appointment of Defence Committee National Defence tell us otherwise, I believe there is some reason for a general suspicion that the motion to set up this committee is a way of sweeping something under the rug for a period of time.
Mr. Speaker, we are approaching the end of the 60 days of decision. I hope the government will on this occasion make the important decision of giving this house and the people of Canada a statement as to their position on the whole question of defence and nuclear weapons.

speechtext: No, one cannot be sure. Orders of the day may be dragged on all day. But we hope that this debate can be ended in orderly fashion. As soon as it has been concluded we shall take the resolution to precede the economic council which, I would hope, if the debate can be focused on the subject, should not take very long. After that we will take the resolution to precede the bill on the department of industry. Should that be completed, the next resolution to be taken tomorrow will be the resolution preceding the bill respecting the Department of Agriculture. I doubt if we shall get beyond that before five o'clock.

At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
